OF MARCUS
ANTONINUS
EMPEROR
TO HIMSELF, BOOKS 12.

OF MARCUS
ANTONINUS
EMPEROR
OF THOSE THINGS WRITTEN TO HIMSELF, 12 BOOKS.

Revised after Gataker and others, and illustrated with notes;
by a most learned man, R. I. of Oxford.

GLASGOW:
AT THE ACADEMIC PRESS,
Printed by R. Foulis, Printer to the Academy.
1744.

To the most noble young man
DUNBAR HAMILTON;
On account of his distinguished zeal,
In ancient literature,
In philosophy,
And in all the good arts,
Whether they pertain to life and character,
Or to the commonwealth,
For their cultivation;
These books
Of the most excellent Philosopher and Emperor alike,
Issuing from the academic press,
To an outstanding alumnus of the Academy,
R. F. A. T. has dedicated.

OF MARCUS ANTONINUS

EMPEROR.

Books to Himself, 12.

OF MARCUS ANTONINUS

EMPEROR,

TWELVE BOOKS.

MARCUS
ANTONINUS
EMPEROR

Book One of His Meditations to Himself

1. From my grandfather Verus: a gentle character and an even temper. 2. From the reputation and memory of my father: modesty and a manly character. 3. From my mother: piety and generosity; and refraining not only from doing evil, but even from entertaining such thoughts. Also, simple living and a way of life far from luxury. 4. From my great-grandfather: not attending public schools, but having good teachers at home; and the understanding that one ought to spend generously on such things. 5. From my tutor: not to be a partisan of the Greens or the Blues at the races, nor a supporter of the light-armed or heavy-armed gladiators; to bear hardship, to want little, to work with one's own hands; to mind one's own business, and to be slow to listen to slander. 6. From Diognetus: not to pursue empty ambitions; to distrust the claims of wonder-workers and sorcerers about spells and the driving away of spirits and such things; not to keep quails for fighting, nor to be excited about such pursuits; to tolerate plain speaking; to become familiar with philosophy; to have listened first to Bacchius, then to Tandasis and Marcianus; to have written dialogues as a boy; and to have desired a simple camp-bed and animal skin, and all such things belonging to the Greek...

MARCUS
ANTONINUS
Emperor

Book I: On Himself

1 From my grandfather Verus I learned to be gentle and meek, and to refrain from anger.
2 From the fame and memory of my father, I learned modesty and manliness.
3 From my mother, I learned piety and generosity: not only to refrain from doing evil, but even from thinking it; likewise to live simply, in a manner far removed from the habits and customs of the wealthy, and to be content with little.
4 From my great-grandfather, I learned to attend public schools, to make use of good private teachers, and to understand that money ought to be spent freely on such things.
5 From my tutor, I learned not to take sides with either the Green or Blue faction in the horse races, nor with the Thracian or Secutor in the gladiatorial contests; to endure hardship; to be content with little; to work with my own hands; to mind my own affairs; never to be quick to listen to slander.
6 From Diognetus, I learned not to spend time on worthless things; not to give credence to the claims of conjurers and sorcerers about incantations, the driving away of evil spirits, and other such impostures; not to keep fighting quails, nor to be seized by a mad fascination for such things; to bear plain speaking with equanimity. To him also I owe my devotion to philosophy, and that I listened first to Bacchius, then to Tandasis and Marcianus; that I wrote dialogues as a boy; and that I desired a camp bed and a rough cloak to sleep on; and other such things.

4 OF MARCUS ANTONINUS

and the other aids of Greek education. From Rusticus, 7
that I came to understand that I stood in need of correction and guidance in my character and conduct; and that I never fell into the ambition and rivalry of the Sophists, whether by composing treatises on speculative subjects, or by declaiming exhortatory speeches, or by showing off my skill in performing exercises and publishing works, in order to draw people into stupefaction and admiration of me; that I likewise abandoned the study of rhetoric, poetry, and the more ornate style of writing; that I did not walk about the house in my toga affecting grandeur, nor do other such things that smack of vanity; that I also wrote letters in a simple manner, following the model of those which he himself had sent from Sinuessa to my mother; that, moreover, I was ready to be appeased and easily reconciled toward those who had given cause for offense or had done something wrong, as soon as they wished to return to good terms; that I read carefully and was not content with a superficial understanding of things, nor did I rashly agree with every idle talker; and finally I owe to him that I read the commentaries of Epictetus, which he himself provided to me from his own library. From Apollonius, I learned to be free; 8 and to maintain a firm and unwavering consistency of judgment and reason, without any fluctuation; and to look to nothing else, however small, except reason alone; and to remain always the same, in the sharpest pains, in the loss of children, in prolonged illness; and moreover, that I saw clearly in him, as in a living example, that one and the same man could be, as occasions demanded, both most energetic and most relaxed; and also that in teaching he was never morose; and that I saw in him a man who clearly showed that he regarded his own skill and cleverness in communicating theoretical knowledge as the least of his good qualities. From him I also learned in what manner one ought to receive what are called favors from friends, so that I would neither become subservient to those received, nor pass them over without any sense of gratitude. From Sextus, a benevolent disposition toward others; and through family 9 affection

Book I. 5

7. Things belonging to Greek education. From Rusticus: learning to recognize that one's character needs correction and care, and not to be led astray into sophistic ambition, nor to write treatises on theoretical subjects, or to deliver little exhortatory speeches, or to show off in a theatrical way the ascetic or the man of leisure; nor to abandon rhetoric or poetry, or refined discourse; and not to walk about the house in formal robes, or do such things; and to write letters in a plain style, such as the one he himself wrote in that manner from Sinuessa to my mother; and to be ready to receive back those who have offended or wronged us, as soon as they themselves wish to return; and to read carefully, and not be satisfied with a general impression, nor quickly to agree with those who talk much; and to have become acquainted with the Memoranda of Epictetus, which he shared from his own copy.

8. From Apollonius: freedom, and being unambiguously without wavering; and to look to nothing else, even for a moment, but to reason alone; and to remain always the same, in sharp pains, in the loss of children, in long illnesses; and to see clearly from a living example that the same man can be both most intense and most relaxed; and not to be impatient in explanations; and to see a man who clearly regarded his experience and skill in transmitting doctrines as the least of his good qualities; and to learn how one ought to receive what appear to be favors from friends, neither being enslaved by them on that account, nor dismissing them with indifference.

9. From Sextus: kindliness; and the example of a household governed by a father's authority; and

6 M. ANTONINI

And the conception of living according to nature; and dignity without affectation; and care for friends with solicitude; and tolerance toward ordinary people, and disregard of those who hold vain opinions; and an approach to all men so agreeable as to be more pleasant than any flattery, while at the same time commanding the deepest respect from those very people at that very moment; and the capacity to grasp, methodically and systematically, the principles necessary for life; and never giving any impression of anger or any other passion, while being at once most free from passion and yet most full of natural affection; and speaking well of others, and this without ostentation; and great learning worn without display. From Alexander the grammarian, the quality of being not reproachful; and not seizing upon those who have spoken something barbarous, or ungrammatical, or ill-sounding in a censorious way, but skillfully introducing only that very expression which ought to have been used, in the manner of an answer, or confirmation, or joint inquiry into the matter itself, not into the word — or by some other such tactful reminder. From Fronto, the lesson to observe what envy, and craftiness, and hypocrisy are as they appear in a tyrant; and that in general those among us who are called men of good family are somewhat lacking in natural affection. From Alexander the Platonist, not to say frequently to someone, or write in a letter, that I am too busy; and not in this way constantly to decline the duties that arise from our relationships with those who live with us, on the pretext of pressing affairs. From Catulus, not to treat lightly a friend who finds fault with something, even if his complaint happens to be unreasonable, but to try to restore the relationship to its usual state; and

BOOK I. 7

...a specimen of fatherly administration: and reflection on how to arrange one's life in accordance with nature: gravity likewise that was in no way affected: and careful attention to friends: and tolerance toward the inexperienced and those who are led by mere opinion without reflection: and manners adapted to any person, so that though his habitual manner surpassed all flattery in its pleasantness, he was nonetheless held in no less reverence by those same persons at that same time: and beyond this, a clear and methodical approach both in the devising and arrangement of such principles as would lead to the right ordering of life: and that I should display no sign of anger or any other agitation; but while being entirely free from passions, I should nonetheless be most inclined toward genuine affection: ready to show favor, but without ostentation: and variously, without display, educated.

10. From Alexander the Grammarian, to refrain from finding fault; and not to reproach anyone scornfully if they have said something barbarous, or grammatically incorrect, or discordant, but to set out deftly only what ought to have been said; doing so under the guise either of answering, or of adding confirmation to what was said, or of jointly examining the matter itself rather than the phrasing, or by means of some other such clever
11. but obliquely executed reminder. From Fronto, to learn what envy, craft, and simulation accompany tyranny: and that those whom we call patricians are for the most part somewhat lacking in genuine affection.
12. From Alexander the Platonist, not to say frequently, nor unless compelled by necessity, either in speech or in writing, that I am too busy; and not in this manner, under the pretext of being heavily occupied with business, habitually to neglect those duties which our bond to one another,
13. according to each person's situation in life, requires of us. From Catulus, not to disregard a friend who complained to me about anything, even if perhaps his complaints had no foundation, but to try to restore him to his former good disposition:

8 M. Antoninus

so that I would praise my teachers readily and generously, as is recorded of Domitius and Athenodotus, and would cherish my own children with sincere affection. From my brother Severus: to love my family; to have a sense of truth and justice; and likewise through him to have come to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion, and Brutus; and to have formed in my mind the idea of a constitution founded on equality and freedom of speech for all, and a monarchy that prizes above all else the liberty of its subjects. From him too I learned to be consistent in my respect for philosophy, to do good promptly, to be generous without reserve, to cherish good hopes, and to have no doubt of the affection of friends; and further, that when he disapproved of anyone's conduct he made no secret of it, and that his wishes and aversions were never difficult for his intimates to guess, but were openly expressed. From Maximus: to be master of myself and not be swayed in any direction; to be of good cheer both in illness and in other adversities; to have a character well-balanced, gentle, and dignified; to carry out the tasks assigned without complaint; and beyond this, to conduct himself so that everyone believed whatever he said came from his honest conviction, and whatever he did was done without ill intent; never to show wonder or astonishment at anything, never to be hurried or sluggish, never troubled, downcast, or given to brooding; never prone to anger or suspicion; always ready to do good and to forgive; always showing himself truthful, and giving the impression of a man who could sooner be corrupted than stand in need of correction; and finally, that no one ever felt looked down upon by him, nor thought himself superior to him; and that he never sought the reputation of being witty. From my father: gentleness, and an unshakable steadiness in decisions once carefully made; in matters generally regarded

BOOK I. 9

The warm praise of teachers, such as I recall about Domitius and Athenodotus; and the genuine affection for his children. From my brother Severus: love of family, love of truth, love of justice; and through him the acquaintance with Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion, Brutus; and the conception of a state with equal laws, governed on the basis of equality and freedom of speech, and of a kingship that above all honors the liberty of its subjects. Also from him: steadiness and consistency in the regard for philosophy; readiness to do good; generosity; hopefulness; and trust in the love of friends; frankness toward those whom he criticized; and the fact that his friends had no need to guess what he wanted or did not want, since it was plain to see.

From Maximus: self-mastery and steadiness; cheerfulness both in general circumstances and in illness; a well-balanced character, gentle yet dignified; diligence in doing what lay before him; the confidence of all who knew him that he meant what he said and did nothing amiss; freedom from wonder and astonishment, never hurrying or hanging back, never at a loss, never dejected, never forcing a smile, yet never angry or suspicious; generosity and a readiness to forgive; giving the impression of straightforwardness rather than of one who has been corrected; the sense that no one ever felt looked down upon by him, nor could anyone suppose himself to be his superior; and a gracious manner.

From my father: gentleness and unshakable adherence to decisions carefully reasoned through; freedom from vanity in regard to so-called honors;

10 M. ANTONINI

honors; and his diligence and perseverance; and his readiness to hear those who had anything to contribute to the common good; and his consistency in rendering to each person what was due according to merit; and his experience in knowing when tension was needed and when relaxation was called for; and his having put an end to the love affairs concerning young boys; and his sense of community; and his allowing his friends neither to dine with him always out of obligation, nor to travel with him under compulsion; and that those who had been absent due to some necessity always found him the same when they returned; and his thoroughness in councils and his persistence, though not one who merely settled for first impressions of the question at hand; and his loyalty in maintaining friendships, never growing weary of them nor being obsessively attached; and his self-sufficiency in all things, and his cheerfulness; and his foresight looking far ahead; and his attention to even the smallest matters without drama; and his checking of excessive gifts and all flattery directed toward himself; and his constant guardianship of what was necessary for governance, and his careful management of resources, and his tolerance of reproach in such matters of administration; and his being neither superstitious toward the gods, nor a crowd-pleaser or flatterer toward men, nor given to popular amusements, but sober in all things and steadfast, never in poor taste or addicted to novelty. And his use, without vanity and without pretense, of those things which fortune provides in abundance and which can lead one astray, so that when present he enjoyed them without affectation, and when absent felt no need of them; and that no one could call him a sophist, or a stay-at-home pampered creature, or a passionate temper, but rather that he was a man of maturity and perfection, beyond flattery, capable of managing both his own affairs and those of others. In addition to these things, his respect for those who were genuinely devoted to philosophy, while not reproaching the others, and furthermore his sociability,

and

Book I. 11

...to yield nothing to empty honors of glory; to be both willing and diligent in bearing burdens; to be ready to hear those who could bring forward anything that might serve the public good; to be turned aside by no one from rendering to each person what he deserved according to his merit; to know well when more vigor was needed and when a more relaxed approach was called for; to restrain himself from the passions of youth; to conduct himself in a thoroughly civil manner; to allow his friends the free choice of dining with him or abstaining, and not to impose on them the obligation of accompanying him when traveling abroad unless they themselves wished to do so; never to be found changed toward those who had been unable to accompany him, even when prevented by some circumstance; in deliberations, to persist steadily in careful inquiry into what needed to be done, and not to abandon the investigation by resting satisfied with whatever appeared obvious on the surface; to be diligent in retaining friends, neither dropping them out of fastidiousness nor clinging to them foolishly; to be content in whatever circumstance fortune placed him, and to maintain a serene countenance; to be prescient of the future from afar, and to be provident in the smallest matters without agitation; to suppress acclamations and all forms of flattery; to watch carefully over what was necessary to the administration, to moderate expenditures with care, and to bear patiently those who criticized him for such things; to be neither superstitious in the worship of the gods, nor, in dealings with men, to seek popular favor through gifts or flatteries, but in all matters to be sober, solid, never foolish, never a lover of novelty. Furthermore, with regard to the things that contributed to a more comfortable passage through life — things fortune supplied to him in the greatest abundance — to use them without ostentation, yet without false restraint, so that he might enjoy what was present in a straightforward way, without greatly longing for what was absent; to be called by no one a sophist, a flatterer, or a pedant, but rather a mature and accomplished man, superior to flattery, fit to manage both his own affairs and those of others. And beyond this, to hold in honor those who truly practiced philosophy, while reproaching no one else.

12 OF M. ANTONINUS

easy and cheerful in company, yet never to the point of excess: to take care of his body with such measured attention that he appeared neither greedy for life nor devoted to elegance, yet not neglectful of it either; but through his own diligence to ensure that he had as little need as possible of physicians' medicines or external remedies. What is most admirable: to yield without envy to those who had distinguished themselves in any field, whether oratory, law, morals, or any other area of knowledge; and moreover to lend them his own effort, so that each might gain the esteem corresponding to those gifts in which they most excelled. Though he carried out everything according to ancestral tradition, he took care not to appear ostentatious in his precise observance of ancestral custom. Furthermore, he was not inclined to be easily moved or to wander, but was accustomed to dwell steadily in the same places and with the same affairs; after his habitual headaches he would return immediately, refreshed and vigorous, to his customary duties: he kept few secrets, indeed very few and very rare, and only such as pertained strictly to public affairs: he showed prudence and moderation in presenting public spectacles, erecting buildings, distributing gifts to the people, and such like matters; since he was one who looked not to gaining fame from his own achievements, but only to what was actually required by the situation. He had no immoderate fondness for baths, no insane passion for building, no fastidious curiosity about food, the weave or dye of clothing, or the appearance of his servants: the toga he used at Lorium was obtained from the lower estate; at Lanuvium he was usually dressed in a simple tunic; in Tusculum he wore a traveling cloak, though he was accustomed to apologize for it: and such was the character of his entire life. Nothing harsh, nothing immodest, nothing violent, nothing that could give rise to what is commonly said, "to the point of sweating": but as if at leisure, with mature deliberation, calmly, quietly, composedly,

and gracious and never sated with it; and his care for his own body was moderate — neither as one who is overly fond of life, nor with an eye to personal adornment, nor yet with neglect — but so that through his own attention he had very little need of medical help, medicines, or external applications. Most especially admirable was his ungrudging willingness to yield to those who possessed some particular ability — for instance in rhetoric, or in knowledge of the laws drawn from history or custom, or in other matters — and his readiness to cooperate with them, so that each might make their mark through their own particular strengths. He always acted in accordance with ancestral custom, and was careful to be seen to do this very thing: to preserve ancestral tradition. Furthermore, he was neither easily moved nor fickle, but was inclined to remain in the same places and engaged in the same affairs; and after attacks of headache he would return fresh and vigorous to his customary work. He had few secrets, and those very few and very rare, and these only concerning public matters. He showed good sense and moderation in organizing spectacles, in managing public works and distributions, and in similar affairs, with his eye fixed on what actually needed to be done, rather than on the reputation to be gained by what was done. He was not one to bathe at unseasonable hours; he was not a builder by passion; he showed no concern for the quality and color of food or clothing, nor for the physical beauty of his attendants. His manner of life came from the estate below, and he spent the greater part of his time at Lanuvium; and how he made use of the customs-collector at Tusculum, and his general conduct of that sort — nothing harsh, nothing inexorable, nothing violent, nothing that one might ever describe as straining to the point of sweat; but everything considered and arranged as if at leisure, calmly, in good order, and with strength. Consistently

in harmony with themselves. That saying remembered of Socrates would well apply to him: that he was able both to abstain from and to enjoy those things, in relation to which many people are weak in abstaining and yielding in their enjoyment. But to be strong and to persevere steadfastly and soberly in both respects belongs to a man who has a perfect and unconquerable soul — as was shown in the illness of Maximus.

From the Gods: to have had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good household members, kinsmen, and friends — nearly everything. And that I never fell into offense against any of them, even though I had a disposition from which, had occasion arisen, I might have done so. It is by the grace of the Gods that no concurrence of circumstances arose which might have put me to the test. And that I was not brought up longer in the household of my grandfather's concubine, and that I preserved my innocence. That I did not come of age too early, but that time was still extended. That I was placed under a ruler and father who was to strip me of all pride, and bring me to understand that it is possible to live in a palace without needing bodyguards, or special garments, or torches, or statues of a certain kind, or similar display; but that it is possible to reduce oneself to nearly the condition of a private person, and yet not thereby to be more abject or more negligent in discharging those duties which the position of authority requires to be performed for the common good. That I had such a brother, who by his character was able to stir me toward care of myself, and who at the same time honored and delighted me. That my children were not born deficient in mind, nor malformed in body. That I did not make further progress in rhetoric, poetry, and the other pursuits in which I might perhaps have become absorbed.

BOOK I. 15

all things consistently and harmoniously disposed in accordance with one another. Thus there applied to him what is said of Socrates: that he knew both how to abstain from and how to enjoy those things from which most people are unable to abstain without weakness, or to enjoy without excess. To be able to show oneself restrained in the one case and temperate in the other is truly the mark of a man endowed with a perfected and unconquerable spirit — as he showed himself finally during the illness of Maximus.

7. I render thanks to the gods that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good companions, good kinsmen and friends, and nearly all good things. Further, that against none of them did I rashly commit any offense, even though I was of such a disposition that, had occasion arisen, I might have done something of the sort. It was by divine grace that no occasion arose through the concurrence of circumstances that would have drawn out that tendency. That I was not brought up for too long in my grandfather's concubine's household; that I preserved the flower of my youth unspoiled, and did not prove my manhood before the proper time, but even delayed it beyond what was necessary. That I was subject to a ruler and father who was to strip me of all arrogance, and who made it credible that it is possible to live at court without needing a bodyguard, or more distinguished clothing, or torches and statues and such things, and similar pomp: but that a ruler can so conduct himself as to come very close to the manner of a private citizen, without on that account being any the less vigorous or lax in carrying out those duties which the state requires in the manner befitting an emperor. That I obtained such a brother, who by his own character could stir me to care for myself, and who at the same time delighted my spirit with his respect and affection for me. That my children were not born dull of mind nor misshapen in body. That I did not make greater progress in rhetoric, poetry, and other such studies, which might perhaps have detained me, ensnared, had I prospered greatly in them —

16 M. ANTONINUS

...that I had benefited from it. That I advanced my foster-fathers to honors which they themselves seemed to desire, without delay, while they were still young, not putting it off with the hope that I would do so later. That I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, and Maximus. That concerning the manner of living according to nature, I had sufficiently clear and frequent thoughts in my mind: so that, as far as the gods are concerned, and their suggestions, aids, and inspirations proceeding from them, nothing at all prevents me from living forthwith according to nature's prescription, unless I myself am finally at fault for not heeding the gods' warnings and their not entirely obscure precepts. That my body has lasted so long through the kind of life I have led. That I never touched Benedicta or Theodotus; and that afterward, when I fell into amorous passions, I recovered my health. That, though I was often angry with Rusticus, I never went so far as to do anything I would have cause to regret. That my mother, though she was to die young, nevertheless spent her last years of life with me. That whenever I wished to help some poor or otherwise needy person, I was never told that I lacked the money to do it; and that I never came into such necessity as to have to borrow from another. That I found in my wife one so obedient, so loving, and so simple. That I was provided with suitable people to raise my children. That remedies were revealed to me in dreams, both in other matters and against the spitting of blood and dizziness of the head: as happened also at Gaeta. That when the desire for philosophy came upon me, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, nor did I waste my time idly in poring over books, or resolving syllogisms, or puzzling over meteorological questions. For all these things required the help of the gods and of Fortune.

Written among the Quadi, on the River Gran.

BOOK

BOOK I. 17

That I did not waste myself in unseemly ways. That I managed in time to settle my nurses in a position of honor, which they seemed to desire of me, rather than putting it off with the hope of doing it later, when they were still young. That I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, and Maximus. That I was shown clearly and often what a life according to nature truly is, so that, as far as the gods are concerned, and their influences, inspirations, and promptings from above, nothing prevented me from living according to nature even then — if I still fell short, it was my own fault, for not keeping to the reminders, or rather the teachings, of the gods. That my body held out so long through such a way of life. That I did not touch Benedicta or Theodotus, and that later, when I fell into amorous passions, I was cured of them. That though I was often angry with Rusticus, I never did anything I would have had to regret. That my mother, though destined to die young, nevertheless lived her last years with me. That whenever I wished to help someone in poverty or in some other need, I was never told I lacked the means to do so; and that I myself never fell into a similar need of receiving the like from another. That my wife was so obedient, so philosophical, and so unaffected. That I never lacked suitable nourishment for my children. That through dreams remedies were given to me — among others, how not to spit blood and not to suffer from vertigo, and this was confirmed at Caieta as if by oracle. That when I turned to philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, nor sat down to analyze texts or work through syllogisms, or busy myself with meteorological speculations. For all these things require the aid of the gods and of fortune.

Written at Granua among the Quadi.

18 M. ANTONINI

BOOK II.

Say to yourself at dawn: I shall encounter today meddlesome, ungrateful, insolent, treacherous, envious, and unsociable people. All these qualities have come upon them because of their ignorance of what is good and evil. But I, having perceived the nature of the good — that it is beautiful — and of the evil — that it is shameful — and the nature of the wrongdoer himself, that he is akin to me, not of the same blood or seed, but sharing in the same mind and divine portion, I cannot be harmed by any of them. For no one can involve me in what is shameful. Nor can I be angry with one who is my kinsman, nor hate him. For we have come into being for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of upper and lower teeth. To work against one another is therefore contrary to nature; and to feel indignation and to turn away from another is to work against him.

Whatever I am, I consist of a little flesh, a little breath, and the ruling mind. Put aside your books; no longer be distracted by them — it is not granted. But as one already dying, despise the flesh: blood and bones, and a fine-woven net of nerves, veins, and arteries. Consider too what the breath is: mere wind, and not even always the same, but every moment expelled and again drawn in. The third, then, is the ruling mind. Reflect thus: you are an old man; let this ruling part no longer be enslaved, no longer be pulled like a puppet by selfish impulse, no longer be vexed at what fate has assigned, whether present or yet to come.

BOOK II.

1 Remember to say to yourself in the morning: Today I will encounter someone who is meddlesome, ungrateful, insolent, deceitful, envious, or selfish. All these faults come upon them through ignorance of what is good and what is evil. But I, who have come to know the nature of the good — that it is honorable — and of the evil — that it is dishonorable — and also the nature of the wrongdoer himself, that he is akin to me, not so much by sharing the same blood and seed, but by partaking of the same mind and share of the divine, I know that none of these people can harm me. For no one can involve me in anything dishonorable. Nor can I be angry with one who is my kin, or hate him. For we are born for cooperation, like feet, hands, eyelids, and the upper and lower rows of teeth. To work against one another is therefore contrary to nature. And to be irritated with someone and to turn away from them is indeed to work against them.

2 Whatever I am consists entirely of a little flesh, a little breath, and the ruling faculty. Therefore, put aside your books: do not let yourself be distracted any further — nothing prevents you from doing so — but rather, as if you were about to die at any moment, despise this flesh: it is blood, little bones, and a network woven from nerves, veins, and arteries. Consider also what the soul is: it is breath, or air; and not always the same, but continually exhaled and drawn back in again. The third element remains: the ruling faculty. Consider then: you are an old man; do not allow that ruling part of you to be enslaved any longer; do not let it be dragged about by impulses contrary to human fellowship; do not resent fate, whether present
3 or yet to come, with fear. The works of the gods...

20 M. ANTONINUS

All things are full of providence. Nor do the things that happen by fortune come about without the help of nature, or without connection and interweaving with those things that are dispensed by providence. From this all things flow: there is added also a certain necessity, and the utility of the whole world, of which you are a part. Now that which the nature of the whole brings forth is good for each part, and whatever conduces to the preservation of that whole. Furthermore, changes of the elements, and likewise of the things composed from them, preserve this world. Let these principles suffice for you; let them ever stand in place of fixed doctrines. Quench your thirst for books, so that you may not die grumbling, but truly at peace and grateful to God from your heart. Remember how long you have been putting these things off, and how many times you have neglected the opportunities offered to you by the gods. Let this be your constant care and concern: that whatever lies at hand, you perform vigorously, as befits a Roman and a man, with genuine — yet not affected — seriousness, humanity, freedom, and justice; and that you meanwhile draw your mind away from all other thoughts. You see how few are the things which, if a man holds to them, he is permitted to live a prosperous and almost divine life. [Section 10] Theophrastus, in his comparison of offences — as one might compare such things in a more general way — says, philosophically, that sins committed through desire are graver than those committed through anger. Rightly, and in a manner worthy of philosophy, he said that what is done with pleasure deserves greater blame than what is done with pain. For what comes from the gods deserves reverence on account of virtue; what comes from men deserves affection on account of kinship; and sometimes it is even pitiable, on account of ignorance of good and evil — and this blindness is no less than that of one unable to distinguish white from black.

Even if you are going to live three thousand years, or thirty thousand times that, 14 remember nonetheless that no one loses any other life than the one he is now living, nor does anyone live any other life than the one he loses. And so the longest and the shortest come to the same thing. The present moment is equal for all; what is lost is not equal; and what is cast away proves to be but an instant. For no one can lose either the past or the future — how could anyone take from you what you do not possess? Remember then two things: first, that all things from eternity are of like form and cycle round, and it makes no difference whether one sees the same things in the span of a hundred years, or two hundred, or in infinite time; and second, that the one who lives longest and the one who will die soonest lose an equal thing — for it is only the present moment one is about to lose, since that is all one has, and what one does not have, one cannot lose.

The human soul injures itself: first, when it becomes, as far as it can, an abscess and a kind of tumor on the world, cutting itself off from nature, in some part of which the nature of each and every other thing is contained — this happens to one who is offended by something that comes his way. 16. The soul of a human being abuses itself, above all when it becomes, as far as it can, an abscess or tumor upon the world. For to feel vexed at anything that happens is a defection from Nature, of which each of the other natures forms a part. Then, again, it abuses itself when it turns against any person or moves against them as an enemy seeking to harm them, as happens with those who are angry. Third, it abuses itself when overcome by pleasure or pain. Fourth, when it acts or speaks in a feigned, artificial, or insincere manner. Fifth, when it directs any act or impulse of its own toward no goal, but acts randomly and without attention to what it does — since even the smallest things ought to be done with reference to the final end. And the end of rational beings is to follow the reason and law of the oldest of cities and constitutions.

17. In human life, time is a point; existence, a flux; perception, dim; the whole composition of the body, prone to decay; the soul, a spinning top; fortune, hard to discern; and fame, a thing without judgment. To put it briefly: everything of the body is a river; everything of the soul, dream and smoke; life is a warfare and a sojourn in a strange land; and posthumous fame is oblivion. What then is able to guide us? One thing and one alone: philosophy. And this consists in keeping the inner spirit free from outrage and harm, superior to pleasures and pains, doing nothing at random, nothing falsely or with pretense, needing nothing from another — whether another acts or refrains from acting; and furthermore, accepting what happens and what is allotted as coming from the same source from which one came oneself. We must reflect not only that each day our life is consumed and a smaller portion of it remains, but also this: that if a person lives longer, it is uncertain whether the mental powers will remain equally capable of understanding things, and of pursuing that contemplation which aims at knowledge of divine and human affairs. For if a man begins to lose his mind, his respiration perhaps, his digestion, his imagination, his appetites, and all such functions will not fail; but that power by which he can make use of himself, fulfill all the duties of his station, clearly express what he has conceived in his mind, consider whether he ought to put an end to his own life, and reflect upon all such matters as require a well-exercised reason — this power, I say, will be utterly extinguished. We must therefore make haste, not only for the reason that we draw closer to death with every passing moment, but also for this further reason: that our capacity to understand and reflect upon things often abandons us before death itself does. It is also worthy of observation, that what arises naturally upon things that are produced by nature also possesses a certain grace and beauty of its own. For instance, when bread is being baked we see certain cracks forming in it; and yet these breaks and openings, though contrary to the art of baking, have a certain pleasing appearance and in their own way stimulate the desire to eat. Figs too, when fully ripe, burst open. And in olives that are nearly overripe, that very quality which borders on decay lends the fruit a certain peculiar charm. 1 One must consider not only this — that life is consumed day by day, and an ever smaller portion of it remains — but also this: that even if a person lives longer, it is uncertain whether his mind will remain equally capable of understanding affairs, and of the contemplation that leads to experience of both divine and human things. And the scowling brow of a lion, or the foam flowing from a boar's mouth, and many other such things — if one were to examine them separately, they would seem far from beautiful, yet because they follow naturally from nature's processes, they add a certain charm and attraction. So that if a person had a genuine feeling and deeper understanding of the things that happen in the universe, almost nothing would fail to appear to him as having its own pleasing quality, following as a natural consequence. In the same way one will view with no less pleasure the actual gaping jaws of wild beasts than what painters or sculptors show in imitation. And with one's own temperate eyes one can perceive a certain ripeness and charm even in an old woman or an old man, and the attractiveness present in all things. Many such things, persuasive to anyone, will present themselves only to the person who has genuinely made himself at home with nature and her works.

Hippocrates, having cured many diseases, himself fell sick and died. The Chaldeans foretold the deaths of many, and then fate overtook them in turn. Alexander, Pompey, and Gaius Caesar, having utterly destroyed whole cities so many times, and cut down many tens of thousands of cavalry and infantry in battle — they too at last departed from life. Heraclitus, who discoursed so much about the conflagration of the universe, died after being filled internally with water and plastered with cow-dung. Democritus was killed by lice, and Socrates was killed by other lice. What does all this mean? You embarked, you sailed, you have come to port — disembark. If it is to another life, there is nothing devoid of the gods, not even there. If it is into unconsciousness, you will cease to endure pains and pleasures, and to serve a vessel so much inferior to what serves it. For what remains is this: one part is mind or spirit, the other is earth and corruption.

and willingly devotes care to all people of whatever kind: if with a mind so disposed you perceive all other lower and meaner things for what they are, you will yield no place to anything else, toward which, if your mind inclines and you lean at all, it will obstruct that good which is properly and peculiarly your own, and prevent you from cultivating and preferring it freely: for to a good that is rational and directed toward the public interest, nothing external can rightly stand in opposition — not, for instance, popular opinion, power, wealth, or a life of pleasure. For all these things, if they seem to offer even the slightest advantage, will immediately prevail and carry you away. But you must simply and freely choose what is best, and cling to it strenuously. What is truly profitable prevails. Therefore, if it shall seem profitable to you, retain it insofar as you are endowed with reason; if not, reject it insofar as you are merely a creature of instinct; and take care to keep your judgment uncorrupted, so that it is not led astray by the outward appearance and surface of things, that you may examine matters with greater precision. Never set value on anything as useful if it drives you to break faith, to abandon modesty, to hate anyone, to be suspicious of anyone, to curse anyone, to dissemble, or to desire anything that requires walls and curtains to conceal. For the man who has placed his own mind and spirit, and the sacred rites of this virtue, before all other things, creates no tragedy, utters no groans, needs neither solitude nor company: and what is most important, he will live without either seeking or fearing death; and he will not think it matters in the least whether his soul dwells in his body for a longer or shorter span of time — since he is one who, if he must depart at once, is as ready to go as to perform any other act that ought to be done with propriety and grace. Throughout his whole life he is scrupulously on guard against one thing: that his mind not evade any of those duties which are proper to a rational and social being. In the soul of a man disciplined and purified, nothing festering, nothing impure, nothing deceitful

...having humbled himself, and caring for other people: if then all other things are judged lesser and more imperfect, give no room to anything else; for having once inclined and turned toward that good which is your own and personal, you will no longer be able, by wandering about carelessly, to maintain it. For it is not lawful to set against the rational and creative good anything of a different kind, such as the praise of the many, or offices, or wealth, or the enjoyments of pleasures. All these things, even if they seem for a moment to fit together, suddenly take hold and carry one away. But you, I say, choose simply and freely what is better, and hold fast to it. The better is the advantageous: if it be the good as pertaining to a rational being, keep to that; if it be the good as pertaining to an animal merely, declare it so, and without vanity guard the judgment alone, so that you may safely conduct the examination. Never esteem as advantageous to yourself that which will someday compel you to break faith, to abandon self-respect, to hate anyone, to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, or to desire things that require walls and curtains. For he who has chosen his own ruling principle and divine spirit, and the sacred rites of that virtue, makes no tragedy, does not groan, has no need of either solitude or crowds. Greatest of all, he lives neither pursuing nor fleeing anything. Whether the soul is to be contained in the body for a longer or shorter span of time, he cares not at all; and if it is already time to depart, he withdraws as easily as he would perform any other act that can be done with decency and order — taking care throughout his whole life of this one thing alone: that his understanding should remain in a manner befitting a rational, social being. 42 Marcus Antoninus

nor lofty would you find it. Nor let fate overtake him in life — as one might say of a tragic actor — before he has completed and acted out his part, and taken his departure. Moreover nothing is conspicuous, nothing elegant, nothing binding, nothing separated off, nothing accountable, nothing hollow. Revere the power of forming judgments. In this lies everything, so that your governing faculty may no longer produce impressions inconsistent with nature and with the constitution of a rational being. This faculty promises freedom from rashness, and affection toward our fellow men, and obedience to the gods. Having cast all else aside, hold fast to these few things only; and remember further that each person lives only the present moment, the merest instant; the rest is either already lived or uncertain. The span that each person lives is small; small too is the corner of the earth in which he lives; small also is the longest posthumous fame, and that too passes along a succession of little men who will themselves soon die, who know not even themselves, much less one who died long ago.

To the marks already mentioned, add yet one more: always to define or sketch the impression that presents itself, so as to see it as it truly is in its essence, stripped bare, whole and entire, and to say to yourself its proper name, and the names of the elements from which it was compounded and into which it will be dissolved. For nothing is so productive of greatness of mind as the ability to examine methodically and truthfully each of the things that present themselves in life, and always to look at them in such a way as to consider at the same time what kind of universe this is, what use this thing serves, what value it has in relation to the whole, and what value in relation to man — who is a citizen of the highest city, of which all other cities are like households — what it is, and of what elements composed,

Book III. 43

do not give offense by trickery. Nor indeed has fate ever cut short a life of this man before its completion, any more than one might say an actor left the stage before the play was finished. Nor will you find in him anything servile, or affected, or enslaved, or cut off, or anything that shuns scrutiny, or that requires concealment. Revere the faculty of judgment. For in this all things are grounded: that no thought dwell in your mind which is inconsistent with the nature of a rational living being. This demands that we decide nothing rashly, that we be well-disposed toward our fellow human beings, and obedient to the gods. Setting aside all other things, keep these few points in mind: and remember moreover that each person lives only in the present moment, which is no more than a point in time; the rest of time is either already past, or lies in an entirely uncertain future. Brief, therefore, is each person's life; narrow the corner of the earth in which he lives; brief too, even when it lasts longest, is posthumous fame — and that fame is passed along by a succession of little men who will die soon enough, who know not even themselves, let alone one who died long ago. To those salutary precepts I have already given, let this one be added: that a definition or description should always be formed of whatever falls under our thought, so that we may see it plainly as it is, stripped bare to its essential nature, whole and entire in all its parts, and judge clearly what sort of thing it is; and that we reflect within ourselves what is its proper name, what are the names of the elements of which it is composed, and into what elements it will in turn be resolved. For nothing so much fosters greatness of mind as the ability to examine honestly and accurately each of the things that arise in life, and always to view them in such a way that one simultaneously considers what place this thing holds in the universe, what dignity it possesses in relation to the whole, and what it means for a human being who acts as a citizen of that supreme city, of which all other cities here below are, as it were, mere households: what it is,

44 M. ANTONINUS

what it consists of and from what principles it is formed, and how long by nature it is destined to last — that which produces in me an impression of present things; likewise, by what virtue one deals with it: whether by gentleness, say, or courage, or truth, or faithfulness, or simplicity, or frugality, or some other quality. Of each thing, therefore, one must say: this came by divine will; this came through a chain and web of fate, or through some such chance concurrence; this came from a fellow tribesman, kinsman, or companion, who does not himself know what accords with his own nature. But since I do know, I treat him with goodwill and justice, in accordance with the law of fellowship that nature has laid down; yet in the meanwhile I take account of the true worth of each of these things. If, having properly followed reason in whatever now presses upon you, you have acted diligently, vigorously, and calmly, and have not looked beyond your set task for anything accessory, but have kept your guiding spirit pure and intact, as if you were about to render it back at any moment — if, I say, you hold to this, expecting nothing further and fleeing nothing, but content to act according to nature's dictate in whatever is at hand, and to speak truth freely in all your words with a heroic spirit, you will live well indeed. And there is no one who can prevent you from doing this. Just as surgeons always keep their instruments and tools ready at hand for sudden treatments, so too should you keep your principles ready, so that you may discern both divine and human matters, and carry out every task, however small, mindful that these two things are interconnected. For in what concerns humanity, you will do nothing rightly without regard to divine things, and vice versa. Do not wander any longer; for it will not come to pass that you will read through your notebooks, or the deeds of the Romans and ancient Greeks, or the excerpts from various authors that you set aside for your use in old age. Hasten therefore to the end, and letting go of vain hopes,

of what things it is composed, and how long it is in its nature to endure — this thing which is now producing an impression on me — and what virtue is required in dealing with it, such as gentleness, courage, truthfulness, faithfulness, simplicity, self-sufficiency, and the rest. Just as physicians always keep their instruments and knives at hand for emergencies in treatment, so keep your principles ready for understanding things divine and human, and for doing even the smallest thing with the awareness of the bond connecting both to each other. That part which holds the ruling power within us, when it has conducted itself according to nature in relation to the things that happen, is so disposed that it can readily adapt itself to whatever is possible and permitted. For it is not attached to any particular material, but moves toward its proposed objects with a condition of reservation; and whatever opposes it in place of those objects, it treats as material upon which to exercise itself — just as a stronger fire, when it seizes upon things that fall in its way or are thrown upon it, things that would quickly have extinguished a feeble flame, turns them to its own advantage and consumes them, and from them draws increased strength. Let nothing be done rashly or carelessly, but only in such a way as to respond most precisely to the rules of the art. People seek retreats for themselves — country houses, shores, mountains — and you yourself are very much inclined to desire such places. But this is altogether the mark of the most common sort of men, when in fact you may retire into yourself whenever you please. For nowhere does a man find a retreat more peaceful or less troubled than in his own soul — especially if he has within himself the kind of things upon whose contemplation he may at once attain complete tranquility; and by tranquility I mean nothing other than that which consists in the well-ordered state of the mind. Make constant use of this retreat, then, and renew yourself. Keep close at hand certain brief and fundamental principles, which, as soon as they come to mind, may cleanse away all distress of soul and send you back free from discontent to whatever you return to. For what is there, indeed, that you ought to bear with distress? The wickedness of men? Bearing in mind that principle — that men, one toward an-

1 The ruling principle within, when it is in accordance with nature, stands in such a relation to events that it can always easily adapt itself to what is possible or given. For it has no attachment to any predetermined material; rather, it moves toward its primary objects with reservation; and whatever is introduced it makes into its own material — just as fire does when it masters what falls into it, by which a small lamp would have been extinguished, while a great flame most swiftly makes its own whatever is heaped upon it, consumes it, or rises yet higher by means of it.

2 Let no action be done at random, nor otherwise than in accordance with a principle that completes the art of living.

Nowhere can a person withdraw to a more peaceful and trouble-free retreat than into his own soul — especially one who has within himself such things that by looking into them he enters at once into a state of perfect ease. By ease I mean nothing other than good order. Continually, then, grant yourself this retreat and renewal. Let the principles you return to be brief and fundamental — enough, when you encounter them, to wash away all distress and send you back without resentment to the life to which you return. Living beings exist for the sake of one another; and that to bear with others is part of justice; and that people sin unwillingly; and how many who have fallen into enmity, suspicion, hatred, and bitter quarreling now lie stretched out and turned to ashes — stop this once and for all. But perhaps you are vexed at what is distributed to you from the whole of things — refresh yourself by recalling the argument, whether it be providence or atoms, and from how many proofs it was shown that the universe is, as it were, a city. But the little glory — are you caught up in it? Look toward the swiftness of universal forgetfulness, the abyss of infinite time on either side, the emptiness of all resounding praise, the fickleness and lack of judgment in those who seem to praise us, and the narrowness of the place in which you are circumscribed. For the whole earth is silent — and how small a corner of it is this dwelling of ours? And here, how many people are there, and of what sort, who will praise you? From now on, then, remember to withdraw into this little domain of your own self; and above all, do not strain or struggle, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal creature. Among the things most ready at hand for refreshment, keep these two. First, that things do not touch the soul, but stand outside it, still and unmoved; while our disturbances come only from the inner judgment. Second, that all these things you see will change almost immediately and will no longer exist; and keep continually in mind how many changes you have already witnessed yourself. The universe is change; life is judgment. If the rational faculty is common to us all, then also reason...

we are said to share in reason in common. If reason, then even that which prescribes what is to be done and what is to be omitted, is reason held in common. If this is so, then the law too is held in common. If this is granted, we are fellow citizens; and given this, we are participants in some form of government; and consequently, the world is like a city. For what other polity could anyone conceive, in which the entire human race is a participant? From where else, then, do we derive the capacity to act with understanding, with reason, and indeed according to law, if not from that common city? For just as whatever is earthy in me has come to me from some portion of the earth; whatever is moist, from a different element; whatever is airy, from its own source; and whatever is warm and fiery likewise from some particular source — (for nothing comes from nothing, nor returns to nothing) — so too does the intellect flow from somewhere.

Death is something like birth; both are mysteries of nature. 5 There is a coming-together from the same elements in one case, and a dissolution back into them in the other — nothing whatsoever in this to cause anyone shame. 56 — Of Marcus Antoninus

All of this is spread abroad among those who are astonished, and who are themselves soon extinguished, so that the memory itself is entirely put out. But suppose those who remember you were immortal, and that your memory too were immortal — what would that mean to you? I speak not now of the dead, but what does praise do for the living survivor? Unless perhaps it serves some purpose of a certain dispensation? For you are untimely abandoning what nature has placed within you, while in the meantime you hang upon the words of others. A good thing of any kind, chapter 20, is good of itself and is complete within itself, and has no part that consists in praise. Therefore it is made neither better nor worse by being praised. I say this also of those things commonly called good in everyday speech — for instance, material things and the works of the arts. That which is truly good, then, needs nothing further, any more than law, truth, benevolence, or modesty. For is any of these made good by praise, or corrupted by blame? Does an emerald become worse if it is not praised? What of gold, ivory, purple, a dagger, a little flower, a small shrub? If souls endure forever, chapter 21, how has the air contained them all from eternity? And how does the earth hold all the bodies that have been deposited in it through so vast an age? For just as bodies here, after remaining in the earth for some span of time, change and dissolve and make room for other corpses: so too souls, transferred into the air, after persisting there for a time, are transformed, dissolved, and kindled, being absorbed back into the universal seminal principle — and in this way make room for others to be received in the same dwelling places. This is the reply one may give if it is granted as a premise that souls survive their bodies. Moreover, one must reckon not only the multitude of bodies buried in this manner, but also the animals that are daily consumed both by us and by beasts.

[22] Do not be distracted, but on every impulse render what is just, and on every impression preserve the faculty of understanding. [23] All that suits you suits me, O World. Nothing is too early or too late for me that is timely for you. Everything your seasons bring is fruit to me, O Nature. From you are all things, in you are all things, to you all things return. That man says, "O beloved city of Cecrops!" — will you not say, "O beloved city of Zeus?" [24] "Do few things," it is said, "if you would not be troubled." But is it not better to do what is necessary, and as much as the reason of a naturally social being prescribes, and in the way it prescribes? For this brings not only freedom from the dejection that comes from acting well, but also from that which comes from doing little. Since most of what we say and do is unnecessary — if a person removes these, he will have more leisure and be less disturbed. Therefore one ought at every moment to remind oneself: "Is this one of the things that is necessary?" And one must remove not only unnecessary actions but also unnecessary impressions, for then no unnecessary actions will follow. [25] Try whether the life of a good man suits you — one who is content with what is allotted to him from the whole, and satisfied with his own just action and benevolent disposition. [26] Have you seen those things? Look at these also. Do not trouble yourself. Unfold yourself. If someone errs, he errs against himself. Has something good happened to you? It was destined for you from the beginning of all things, and all that comes to pass was woven together with it. And in sum: life is short.

...those who died ungracefully, grumbling about their circumstances, loving, hoarding, craving consulships and kingdoms. That life of theirs is now nowhere to be found. It is necessary to remember this: that attention given to each action has its own proper value and proportion. Thus you will not be dissatisfied, unless you dwell more than is fitting on lesser matters. The expressions once in common use are now archaic glosses. So too the names of those once much celebrated are now in a manner mere obsolete words: Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Leonnatus, and shortly after Scipio and Cato, then Augustus, then Hadrian and Antoninus. All things fade quickly and become the stuff of legend; and soon complete oblivion buries them. And this I say of those who shone in some remarkable way. The rest, as soon as they breathe their last, are unknown and unheard of. What then is there at all that is worth remembering forever? Utterly nothing. What then is it about which we ought to apply ourselves with earnestness? This one thing: a just mind, actions directed toward the common good, speech that never deceives, and a disposition that welcomes whatever happens as necessary, as familiar, as flowing from the same source and spring. Willingly surrendering yourself to Clotho, allowing her to spin you together with whatever events she wills.

68 M. Antoninus

How many have discoursed at such length about death and immortality; how many brave warriors, after slaying multitudes, have themselves been slain; how many tyrants, who wielded the power of life and death over others as though they stood beyond the reach of death, exercised it with terrible arrogance — and then perished themselves; how many cities too, if I may say so, have died: Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and countless others. Go through likewise all those you yourself have known, who one after another buried each other, and were at last themselves carried out — and how brief a span of time contained all of this. The sum of it comes to this: that you should always look upon all human things as fleeting and worthless — for what was yesterday's mucus becomes tomorrow's ash or dust. So pass through this indivisible moment of time in a way suited to nature, and depart from it graciously — just as a ripe olive falls, praising the nature that bore it and giving thanks to the tree from which it came.

Be like a headland against which the waves crash continually, yet it stands firm and tames the foaming waters around it. "How unfortunate I am," says someone, "that this has happened to me." On the contrary — how fortunate I am, that although this has happened, I feel no pain, am not broken by the present, nor do I dread the future. For something like this could have happened to anyone; but not everyone could have borne such a misfortune without distress of mind. Why then is this circumstance counted as misfortune rather than as good fortune? Can you call it a man's misfortune when it does not prevent human nature from achieving its proper end? And does that thing, as it seems to you, prevent human nature from achieving its proper end, when it does not happen contrary to that nature's own will? And what that will is, it is not for you to learn now. But can any circumstance prevent you from being just, magnanimous, temperate, prudent, free from rash assent, free from error, modest, and free, and whatever else human nature in its fullness possesses when all these qualities are present? Remember henceforth, whenever anything befalls you —

In the morning, when you rise with reluctance, let this thought be ready to hand: I am rising to do the work of a human being. Why then should I be resentful, if I am going out to do what I was born for and brought into the world to do? Or was I made for this — to lie in bed wrapped in blankets and keep myself warm? But this, you say, is more pleasant. Were you born then for pleasure? Were you not born for action and exertion? Do you not see the little shrubs, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees, each working at its own station in the world, doing its part to maintain the order of nature? And you — do you refuse to do what belongs to a human being? Do you not hasten toward that which is suited to your nature? But rest too is necessary, you say. I grant it; but nature has set a limit to rest, just as it has set a limit to eating and drinking. Yet you go beyond that limit, beyond what is sufficient, in these things. In your actions, however, you fall short of what you could do, and hold yourself back. The truth is, you do not genuinely love yourself — for if you did, you would love your nature and what your nature requires. and to be at once in complete serenity. Count yourself worthy of every word and action according to nature; and do not let the blame or censure of certain people lead you astray.
