There is also one who, in a sense, does not even know what he has done; but he is like a vine which, when it has produced its cluster of grapes and yielded its own fruit once, asks for nothing more. Just as a horse after it has run its race, a dog after it has hunted, a bee after it has made its honey — so this person, after doing good, does not go on making a clamor about it, but moves on to another task of the same kind; just as the vine goes on to produce new clusters in their due season. Should we not then be among those who, in a sense, do not even know what they are doing? That is exactly right. But, you say, it is necessary to understand what you are doing. For it is the mark of one who observes the law of society to feel that he is acting according to that law; and indeed, by Jupiter, to wish that the one toward whom he so acts should also perceive it. That is true, I admit, what you say: yet, as has already been said, if you take it otherwise, you will be among the number of those I mentioned earlier — for they too are led astray by a certain plausible appearance of reason. But if you are willing to understand rightly what I have said, do not fear that you will miss any opportunity of doing good on that account. It was the prayer of the Athenians: "Rain, rain, dear Jupiter, upon the fields and meadows of the Athenians." Either one ought not to pray at all, or one ought to pray in this simple and frank manner. It is similar to what is commonly said — that Aesculapius prescribed for this or that person riding, cold baths, or going barefoot: so too it is when universal nature prescribes for this or that person illness, mutilation of body, loss of children, or something of that sort. For in the former case, "prescribed" means that this was ordained toward that person's health; and likewise here, whatever happens to each person is in some way ordained toward that which is in accordance with fate.

BOOK V. 77

...about some action, he is ready to reckon the favor to himself. But the truly ready man thinks of it differently within himself, as one who reflects on a debt, knowing what he has done. And yet another knows in a certain way what he has done; but he is like a vine that has borne a cluster of grapes and asks nothing more, having once brought forth its own fruit. A horse that has run, a dog that has tracked, a bee that has made honey, a man that has done good — none of these clamor for recognition, but pass on to something else, as the vine passes on to bear its cluster again in due season. Must one be among those who do this in a way, so to speak, without awareness? Yes — but it is precisely this that one must be aware of. For it is characteristic of the social being, as one might say, to perceive that he acts socially, and indeed to wish that his fellow also perceive it. What you say is true; but you are misunderstanding what is now being said, and so you will fall into the class of those I mentioned second — for those people are led astray by a kind of plausible reasoning. But if you wish to understand what is really meant, do not fear that you will thereby neglect any social duty.

The prayer of the Athenians: Rain, rain, O dear Zeus, upon the fields and plains of the Athenians. One ought either to pray simply and freely in this way, or not at all.

It is just like the saying that Asclepius prescribed for someone riding exercise, or cold baths, or going barefoot: in the same way, the nature of the whole has prescribed for someone disease, or mutilation, or loss, or something else of that kind. For in the first case the word "prescribed" means something like "ordered this in relation to that, as fitting for health"; and here too, what befalls each person has been ordered in a way suited to his destiny. For so indeed...

...we say these things happen to us, just as craftsmen say that squared stones in walls or pyramids fit together, harmonizing with one another by a certain kind of arrangement. For on the whole, harmony is one. And just as the universe is made complete from all bodies, so too fate, being such a cause, is made complete from all causes. Even the completely uneducated understand what I am saying. For they say: "This was brought upon him; this was fated for him; this was bound up with him." Let us then accept these things, just as Asclepius prescribes certain remedies. For many of those remedies are harsh, yet we embrace them in the hope of health. Let the completion and fulfillment of what universal nature decrees seem such a thing to you, like your own health. And so embrace everything that comes to pass, even if it seems rather harsh, because it leads there — to the health of the universe, and to the road and purpose of Zeus. For nothing would have been brought about unless it was of benefit to the whole. For no chance nature brings forth anything that is not fitting for what is governed by it. For two reasons you must love what befalls you: first, because it came to you, was bound to you, and was in some way directed toward you, woven from above by the most ancient causes; and second, because it is a cause for the one who governs the whole — of its course, its completion, and, by Zeus, of its very continuance. For the whole is impaired if you sever any part of the connection and continuity, whether of the parts or of the causes. And you do sever it, as far as it is in your power, whenever you are discontented and in a way destroy it. Do not be disgusted, nor despair, nor lose heart, if you do not always succeed in acting according to right principles in every matter; but when you fall short, return again...

It stands thus. And hence it is that we say things fit together for us, in the same way that craftsmen say square stones in walls or pyramids fit together, when they are skillfully joined to one another. For there is altogether one single framework of all things. And just as from all bodies this world, whereby a body of such a kind is completed, is formed; so from all causes, the fate of such a kind is brought about. Even the most unlearned understand what I mean. For they say, "this was brought upon him — his lot, of course." So this was brought upon him, and this was coordinated for him. Let us therefore receive these things in the same way that we are accustomed to receive what Aesculapius has prescribed. For indeed many of his prescriptions are harsh, yet we willingly accept them in the hope of health. Let something of this sort therefore appear to you — the perfection and completion of what has seemed good to universal nature, of which your health is one such instance. And in the same way, whatever happens, however harsh it may seem, accept it willingly, inasmuch as it contributes to the integrity of the world and to the prosperity and happiness of Jupiter. For he would not have brought it about unless it contributed to the good of the whole; since no nature whatsoever brings about anything which is not fitting for that world which is governed by it. Thus you ought to cherish, for two reasons, whatever happens to you. The first, because it was born for you and coordinated for you, and in some way directed toward you, woven back to you from the most ancient causes. The second, because it is a contributing cause to the prosperity, completion, and indeed the preservation of the governor of the universe. For the whole itself is mutilated if you cut off even the smallest thing from its connection and continuity — both of the parts of the universe and of its causes. And you do cut off, as far as it lies in you, whenever you bear something with displeasure and in a sense remove it. Do not be troubled, or lose heart, or be indignant, if it does not always turn out equally well for one who wishes to act according to right principles. But where —

80 MARCUS ANTONINUS

Whenever you feel yourself straying from the path, return to it, and be content with having performed the many duties belonging to human life; and make sure you love that to which you return. Do not go back to philosophy as to a schoolmaster, but as a person with sore eyes flies to the eye-salve and the brush, as another flies to a poultice, and another to a fomentation. In this way you will need nothing further to reconcile you to the dictates of reason, but will yield to them of your own accord. Remember too that philosophy desires only what your own nature desires; whereas you were wishing for something other than what suits your nature. For what could be more agreeable than that? Does not pleasure deceive us in this very way? But consider whether magnanimity, liberality, simplicity, equanimity, and sanctity are not more agreeable. And what could you find more pleasing than wisdom itself, when you reflect on the readiness and smooth working of a faculty equipped with understanding and knowledge, never stumbling, but moving successfully in all things? Indeed, things themselves are so hidden that to many philosophers — and not the least of them — they have seemed wholly incomprehensible; and even to the Stoics they appear very difficult to grasp. And in truth all our assent is liable to change and error. For where is the man who has never at some point changed a mistaken opinion? And if you turn to the things themselves, consider how fleeting and base they are, and how even a debauchee, a prostitute, or a thief might come to possess them. As for the character of those with whom you live, if you observe carefully, you will find it such that you can scarcely endure even the most agreeable of them — to say nothing of each man scarcely being able to bear himself. In such darkness and squalor, then, and in so great a flux of matter, time, motion, and things in motion, I can discover nothing worth esteeming or striving after. Rather, each person would do better to console himself by awaiting the natural dissolution of his being, not chafing at the delay in the meantime, but resting wholly content in these two things: first,

BOOK V. 81

...having been hidden away, to return again and to blend oneself into what is more human and more numerous, and to love that to which one returns; and not to return to philosophy as to a schoolmaster, but as those with sore eyes return to a sponge and an egg, as another returns to a poultice, as to a soothing lotion. For in this way one will show no mere compliance with reason, but true rest in it. Remember that philosophy desires only what your own nature desires; but you were wishing for something else, not in accordance with nature. For what is more agreeable than these things? Is pleasure not bought through error? But consider whether something more agreeable might be greatness of soul, freedom, simplicity, good sense, piety. And what is more agreeable than wisdom itself, when you reflect on the smoothness and the reliability of the faculty of understanding and knowledge in all things?

Things are veiled in such a way that they have seemed to not a few philosophers, and not only ordinary people, to be either utterly incomprehensible — or at least the Stoics consider them hard to comprehend. And all our assent is liable to change; for who is unchangeable? Apply yourself therefore to the things themselves: as short-lived, incomplete, and capable of being occupied by a prostitute or a thief. After this, look at the characters of those who live alongside us, among whom it is hard even for the most agreeable to be tolerated, not to mention that one can barely endure even oneself. In such darkness and filth, and in such a flux of substance and time, and of motion and things in motion, I cannot conceive what there is that is worthy of honor or of earnest pursuit. On the contrary, one must console oneself and wait for the natural dissolution, and not be troubled by the delay, but find rest in these things alone: first, in the thought that...

82 M. Antonini

...because nothing will befall me that is not in accordance with the nature of the whole; and for another reason, because nothing compels me to act contrary to my own god or inner spirit. For there is no one who can force me to transgress it. 11 To what use, then, am I now putting my own soul? At every moment one must ask this of oneself, and examine what it is I now have in that part which they call the ruling faculty — and what kind of soul do I now have? Is it the soul of a child? Of a youth? Of a weak woman? Of a tyrant? Of a beast of burden? Of a wild animal? 12 What sort of things are those considered goods by the many, you may gather from this. If someone were to conceive of certain things as truly good — such as wisdom, temperance, justice, courage — he would not, having first conceived of these, be able even to listen to anything being said to be "under the good," for it would not fit. But if someone first conceives of the things that appear to the many to be good, he will easily hear and readily accept, as fittingly applied, what is said by the comic poet. Thus the many imagine the distinction. For what on the one hand would not have been offensive and would have been rejected — what relates to wealth and to the inheritance of luxuries or of glory we accept as wittily and elegantly said. Go further and ask whether one ought to honor and count as goods such things as these, of which, if first conceived, it would naturally follow that the person possessing them, from sheer embarrassment, would not know where to relieve himself. 13 I am composed of a causal and a material element; neither of these will be destroyed into non-being, just as neither came into being from non-being. Therefore every part of me will by transformation be assigned to some part of the cosmos, and that in turn will change into another part of the cosmos, and so on into infinity. By just such a process of change I too came into being, and those who begot me...

namely, that nothing can befall him which is not in accordance with universal nature; and secondly, that it lies within his own power to do nothing contrary to the will of his own divine spirit and God. For there is no one who can compel him to transgress this. What purpose does my soul now serve? Ask yourself this continually, and at the same time examine yourself: what is now occupying that part of me which is commonly called the ruling part? Or whose soul am I now displaying? That of a child? Of a youth? Of a weak woman? Of a tyrant? Of a beast of burden? Of a wild animal? What the things are that appear good to the majority of people may be gathered from this: if a person conceives in his mind things that are truly good — such as prudence, temperance, justice, fortitude — these, I say, if he has preconceived them in his mind, he will not be able to bear hearing anything applied to them that does not properly suit a true good. But as for those things commonly held to be good, when someone has preconceived them in his mind, he will listen with willing ears and easily accept what a comedian might at some point have said about them, as aptly applied. Even common people have some awareness of this distinction. Otherwise it would not give offence and be rejected as unworthy of utterance, if said of those things, while when said of wealth and the gifts of fortune that lead to luxury and display, we accept it as aptly and cleverly put. One may also inquire whether things of this kind are to be held in honor or reckoned among goods, when, given prior conception of them in the mind, that saying might fitly be applied — that a man so furnished with them lacks, amid all his wealth, a place to lay down the burden of his belly. I am constituted of form and matter: neither of these shall perish into nothing, just as neither proceeded from nothing. Therefore every part of me, as change intervenes, shall be resolved into some part of the universe according to its own nature. And that in turn will be changed into another part of the universe, and so on to infinity. And by such change I myself came into existence, and those who

84 M. Antoninus

who had begotten me, and so back into another infinity. For nothing prevents me from saying this, that even according to cycles, the world is ordered within fixed and definite limits. Reason and the rational faculty itself are self-sufficient for their own works and purposes. They are set in motion from their own principle and proceed from it, and they move in a straight line toward the goal set for them. Hence actions of this kind have rightly received the name of right actions, by which the straightness of the path is indicated. None of these things should be called properly human which do not pertain to a human being as such. For these things are neither required of a human being, nor promised by human nature, nor do they tend toward its perfection. Nor, accordingly, does the end of human nature consist in these things, nor does any good that conduces to the attainment of this end. Furthermore, if any of these things did pertain to a human being, it would not befit a person to hold them in contempt or to oppose them; nor would one be thought worthy of praise for showing oneself to have less need of them. Indeed, a person would not even be considered good who had denied himself any of these things, if they were truly good. But on the contrary, the more a person has stripped away from himself of these and similar things, or has endured with equanimity what has been stripped away by others, the more deservedly is he esteemed. Your mind will become such as are the thoughts you most frequently dwell upon. For the soul is steeped in its thoughts. Steep it, therefore, in thoughts of this kind: for example, that wherever one lives, it is possible to live well there; that it is permitted to live at court — therefore it is also possible to live well at court. And again, that everything has been made for some purpose, and is fitted to act for that purpose; and that toward which it is fitted to act, it is drawn; and toward which it is drawn, there lies its proper end; and where the end of each thing lies, there too lies its utility and good: therefore the good of a rational living being is society. That we are born for this has been demonstrated above. For is it not

BOOK V. 85

...having praised me, and returning to another infinite. Nothing prevents one from saying this, even if the world is governed by a fixed and orderly cycle. Reason and the rational art are powers sufficient unto themselves, and unto their own proper works. Setting out from their own proper principle, they proceed toward the end set before them. And such actions are rightly called correct actions, signifying the rightness of the path. None of these things should be attributed to a human being, as human, that do not properly belong to a human being. These are not things demanded of a human being, nor does human nature promise them, nor are they perfections of human nature. Therefore neither does the end set before a human being lie in these things, nor is the good the fulfillment of that end. Furthermore, if any of these things properly belonged to a human being, it would not be fitting for him to despise them and set himself against them. Nor would one be praiseworthy who showed himself free of need for them. Nor would one who diminished himself in any of these things be good, if indeed they were goods. But as things stand, the more a person strips away from himself these things or others like them, or endures being stripped of some of them, the more good he is.

Whatever you repeatedly imagine, such will be the character of your mind. For the soul is dyed by its impressions. Dye it, therefore, by dwelling continually on such impressions as these: that wherever it is possible to live, it is also possible to live well. But one can live in a palace; therefore one can also live well in a palace. And again: that each thing was made for that for which it was made; toward that it naturally tends; where its tendency leads, there lies its end; where its end is, there too is its benefit and its good. The good of a rational being, therefore, is community. For that we were born for community has long been

86 M. ANTONINI

...has long been shown. Or was it not clear that inferior things exist for the sake of superior things, and superior things for one another? And superior to inanimate things are animate things; and superior to animate things are rational beings. [17] To pursue impossible things is madness; and it is impossible to make base people other than what they are. [18] Nothing happens to anyone that he is not naturally fitted to bear. The same things happen to another, and he either does not know they have happened, or he displays greatness of soul with unaffected composure, or he endures without complaint. It would be strange if ignorance or vanity were stronger than wisdom. [19] External things do not touch the soul at all, nor have any entrance to it; they cannot turn or move it. Only the soul turns and moves itself; and whatever judgments it deems worthy of itself, such are the things it makes for itself as consequences. [20] On one account man is the being most closely related to us, inasmuch as we must do good to men and endure them; but insofar as some men stand in the way of our proper work, man becomes for me one of the indifferent things, no less than the sun, or the wind, or a wild beast. By these, activity may indeed be hindered, but impulse and disposition are not obstructed, because of the power of reservation and adaptability. For the mind circles around or sets aside every obstacle to action, advancing what is preferred; or, when obstructed in action, it turns to what is ready to hand instead; or when blocked on a path, it turns to finding another way along that same road. [21] Honor what is most powerful in the universe; that is the power which makes use of all things and governs all things. Likewise honor what is most powerful in yourself; and this is of the same kind as that universal power. For it is that which makes use of all else in you, and by which your whole life is governed. [22] What is not harmful to the city is not harmful to the citizen...

Book V. 87

For it is quite clear that all inferior things are created for the sake of superior ones, and superior ones for one another. Now animate things surpass inanimate ones, and among animate things, those endowed with reason surpass the rest. [17] To pursue what cannot be done is madness. Yet it cannot but happen that wicked people do certain things of this kind. [18] Nothing happens to anyone that nature has not given him the strength to bear. Others have had the same things befall them — some ignorant of their misfortunes, others eager to show greatness of spirit — and they remained unmoved and unharmed. It is unworthy that ignorance and arrogance should have more power than wisdom. [19] External things cannot in any way touch the soul; they have no access to it, and they cannot change or move it. The soul alone changes and moves itself. Whatever judgments it has made, and whatever place it has given to things within itself, accordingly it shapes all that comes to it from outside. [20] In one respect, man is the being most closely joined to us, insofar as it is our duty to help and sustain our fellow men. Yet insofar as people sometimes stand in the way of our proper actions, in that respect man counts for me among indifferent things, no less than the sun, the wind, or a wild beast. All of these can obstruct my action, but no impediment is given to my effort or disposition, thanks to the power of exception and conversion. For the mind converts and transfers every obstacle to action into the very thing that serves its purpose. Thus it comes about that what hinders this work of mine leads me toward another work, and what stood in the path I had taken becomes a guide to a new path. [21] Of all that the universe contains, honor that which is most excellent — and that is what makes use of all other things and governs all the rest. In the same way, honor what is most excellent in yourself — and that is what is akin to the above, for it is what makes use of all else in you, and by which your life is governed. [22] What is not harmful to the city does not harm the citizen. Toward this...

88                OF M. ANTONINUS

Apply to all these matters the rule of what seems likely to harm you: if the state suffers no harm from it, nor do I; and even if the state were to suffer some harm from it, one should not be angry with the one who injures the state, but should show him in what he is at fault. Often reflect how quickly all things that exist and come into being are swept away and disappear. For the nature of things is like a river in perpetual flow; its effects are subject to continual change, and causes themselves to countless turnings; and there is almost nothing that stands still. Reflect likewise on that vast and boundless expanse of time on either side — past and future — into which all things vanish. Who then could rightly be considered anything but a fool, who is puffed up, or tormented, or complains about something that causes distress for so brief a span, as though it would last long? Remember also the nature of the whole, of which you hold a very small portion; and of time, of which a brief and momentary interval has been assigned to you; and of fate, how small a part of it you are. If someone does wrong against me, that is his concern. He has his own disposition, his own way of acting. I now have what the nature of things wills me to have; and I do what my own nature now wills me to do. That part of your soul which holds the chief command and governance must remain unmoved by any light or rough motion of the flesh; it must not mingle with it, but must confine itself, and keep those passions within the limits of the bodily members. If, however, by some other means they work their way up to the mind — insofar as it is united with the body — then one must not resist what comes from nature by sensation; but the judgment of the ruling part must be brought to a halt, so that it does not pass any verdict on these things as either good or evil. One must live with the Gods. And he will do this who shows his soul continually disposed to accept what is assigned to him, and to do whatever the divine spirit

harms a fellow citizen. Apply this rule to every impression you have of being harmed: if the city is not harmed by this, then neither am I harmed; but if the city is harmed, one ought not to be angry at the one who harms the city.
23. What is being overlooked. Often reflect upon the swiftness with which things that exist and things that come into being are swept away and carried off. For substance is like a river in perpetual flow; activities are in continual change; causes turn in ten thousand ways; and almost nothing stands still, even what is near at hand. And the infinite expanse of past and future is a vast abyss in which all things vanish. How then could anyone be a fool who puffs himself up over these things, or is tormented by them, or makes lamentation, as if they troubled him for some time, even a little?
24. Remember the totality of substance, of which you possess the smallest share; and of the totality of time, of which a brief and fleeting interval has been assigned to you; and of fate, of what portion you are a part.
25. Does another do wrong against me? That is his own affair. He has his own character, his own action. I now have what the common nature wills me to have, and I do what my own nature wills me to do now.
26. The ruling and sovereign part of the soul must remain unaltered by the smooth or rough movements in the flesh, and must not blend with them, but must circumscribe itself and confine those affections to the bodily parts. 27. To live with the gods. He lives with the gods who continually shows them a soul content with what is allotted to it, obedient—

90 M. ANTONINUS

— doing whatever he wishes — the daemon, which Zeus has given to each person as a guardian and guide, an emanation of himself; and this is each person's mind or reason. Will you be angry with the old man? Will you be angry with the one who smells bad? What can he do to you? He has such a body, such armpits — it is necessary that such an emanation arise from such things. But the man has reason, someone says, and is capable of understanding when he offends. Good luck to you then; well, you also have reason — move him by a rational disposition toward a rational disposition; show him, remind him. If he responds, you will cure him, and there is no need for anger. [Neither like a tragic actor, nor like a prostitute.] 29. As you have planned to live once you have gone out into the world, so it is possible to live here too. And if they do not permit it, then depart from life — yet in such a way as one who suffers no evil. "There is smoke, and I leave." What do you think is so remarkable about that? But so long as no such thing drives me out, I remain free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I wish; and I wish to live in accordance with the nature of the rational and social being. 30. The mind of the Whole is social in character. It has made the inferior things for the sake of the superior, and has fitted the superior things to one another. You see how it has subordinated, arranged, and assigned to each according to worth, and brought the most powerful into harmony with one another. 31. How have you conducted yourself up to now toward the gods, your parents, brothers, wife, children, teachers, tutors, friends, relatives, servants? Consider that toward all of them it has been your rule up to now neither to do nor say anything unworthy. Recall also through what things you have passed, and what things you have been strong enough to endure; and that the story of your life is now full and your service complete; and how many beautiful things you have seen; how many pleasures and pains you have looked beyond; how many

Book V. 91

he willed it, Jupiter having torn off a particle of himself assigns to each person a guardian and guide for the future. And this guardian is nothing other than each person's mind and reason. Do you feel anger toward the one who smells of a goat? Or toward the one whose mouth emits a foul breath? What could he do about it? Such a mouth is his, such armpits are his, so that it is inevitable that such odors proceed from each of them. But, you say, a human being is endowed with reason, and if he pays attention, he can recognize his faults. Well and good. Then you too, since you are endowed with reason, use your rational faculty to awaken that same reason in him, point out his error, and remind him of it. For if he listens to you, you will have cured him, and there will be no further need for anger. [Neither a tragedian nor a harlot.] In whatever manner you think to live when you are about to depart this life soon, you may live in that same way now, if you choose. But if those among whom you live do not permit it, then depart from life itself — yet in such a way as one who has suffered no wrong. If smoke troubles me, I leave the room. Why should this be thought a matter of great consequence? Meanwhile, as long as nothing compels me to withdraw, I remain free; for no one can prevent me from doing what I choose: and what I choose is what is in accordance with the nature of a rational being born for society. The mind of the universe is a lover of mutual fellowship. Therefore it has ordered lesser things for the sake of greater, and has bound the greater things to one another. You see how it has subordinated individual things in just order, gathered them together, assigned to each its due according to its dignity, and bound the highest things together by mutual agreement. Recall to yourself how you have conducted yourself up to now toward the gods, your parents, brothers, spouse, children, teachers, educators, friends, intimates, and servants; and whether up to now you have been guilty of anything unworthy in deed or word toward any of them. Recall also what affairs you have transacted, and what burdens you have been sufficient to bear. Consider too that the story of your life is now complete, and that your duty is done. Recall likewise how many noble things you have witnessed; how many pleasures—

92 . Of Marcus Antoninus

how many pleasures and pains you have scorned; how many things held glorious you have disregarded; how many times you have dealt fairly even with the wicked. For what purpose do rude and ignorant souls trouble one who is trained and skilled in the art? But what is the soul that is skilled and trained in the art? It is one that knows the beginning and end of all things, and knows that reason which pervades all things and administers this whole universe through all its appointed cycles of ages. You will very soon be ashes, or bare bones, and your name will survive you — or perhaps not even your name. And a name is nothing but an empty sound and echo. The very things that are so highly prized in this life are empty, rotten, trivial — like dogs snapping at one another, or children quarreling and then laughing one moment and crying the next. But faith, modesty, justice, and truth have departed from the broad earth to heaven. What then keeps you here? If the objects of sense are ever shifting and unstable, our senses themselves are dull and easily deceived by false impressions; the soul itself is a mere exhalation from the blood; and to be famous among such people is an empty thing. Why then do you not await calmly either your extinction or your removal elsewhere? And until that time comes, what is sufficient except to worship the gods and praise them, to do good to men, to bear with them and to refrain from harming them; and to remember that all that lies outside the limits of your poor body and soul is not yours and not in your power? Your affairs will go prosperously for you always, if you are able to proceed rightly and by sound method both in thought and in action. Two things are common to the soul endowed with reason, whether of a god, a man, or any other rational being: first, that it cannot be hindered by anything external; second, that it places its good in a just disposition and action of the soul, and needs to desire nothing beyond this. If neither this vice be mine, nor the effect of vice

How many things of reputed worth have you passed by! Into how many ungrateful people have you poured yourself. Why do unskilled and ignorant souls contain one who is skilled or distinguished? What would a skilled and distinguished soul be? One that knows beginning and end, and the reason that pervades all substance, and through all eternity governs the whole according to appointed cycles.

33. How soon will you be ashes or bare bones, and either a name or not even a name; and a name is mere noise and echo. And the things highly valued in life are empty and rotten and trivial — little dogs snapping at each other, children quarreling and laughing, then straightway weeping. And faith and modesty and justice and truth have departed to Olympus from the wide-wayed earth. What then still holds you here? If the objects of sense are ever changing and never stable; if our senses themselves are dim and easily deceived; if the soul itself is but a vapor from the blood; if to win approval among such people is empty — what are you waiting for? Await with serenity either extinction or removal. And until that time comes, what suffices? What else but to revere the gods and praise them, to do good to men, to bear with them and refrain from wrongdoing, and as for all that lies outside the bounds of this poor flesh and breath, to remember that these things are not yours, nor in your power.

34. You can always find a way forward, if you proceed rightly and by the right road, doing two things common both to God and to every rational living soul: not to be hindered by another, and to hold your good in a just disposition and action, and there to let desire find its end.

Yet the wonder of this craft is that, having set its own boundaries, it transforms back into itself everything within that seems to decay, age, and become useless, and it makes fresh new things again from these same materials — so that it needs no substance from outside, nor has need to discard the more rotten parts. It is satisfied with its own space, its own matter, and its own craft. No man has a stronger or more secure refuge than this, and whoever flees to it can never again fall into the power of another. He who does not see this is foolish; he who sees it and yet does not take shelter there is wretched. Think nothing further within yourself beyond what your first impressions have reported. But that he is in danger — that I do not see. Thus always hold firm to first impressions, add nothing more to them from within yourself, and nothing happens to you that can disturb you. Or rather, add something further: namely, that you have a thorough understanding of the nature of all things that occur in this world. A cucumber is bitter — put it aside. There are thorns in the path — turn away from them. That is enough. Do not go on to say, "Why do such things exist in the world?" For you will be laughed at by one who is skilled in natural science, just as you would be laughed at by a carpenter or cobbler if you criticized their craft because you saw the shavings and offcuts lying about their workshop. And yet they at least have somewhere to throw such waste; but universal Nature has nothing outside herself — yet what is most wonderful in her art is this: having set certain boundaries for herself, she converts back into herself whatever within her seems to decay, grow old, and become useless, and from these same materials produces new things. Thus she has no need of external matter, nor does she need a place to cast away what has rotted. She remains content with her own place, her own matter, and her own art. And be not sluggish in your actions, nor quarrelsome in your dealings, nor wandering in your thoughts, nor let your soul be swept away in rashness and reckless leaping, nor be entangled in life with too many affairs. They kill you, they cut you down, they curse you with dreadful imprecations. What do all these things prevent you from keeping your mind pure, prudent, sober, and just? Evil in general does no harm to the universe. 55 In particular it harms no one else either. It is harmful only to the one to whom it has been granted to be free from it, whenever he himself wills it. In my judgment, 56 the free choice of my neighbor is, on equal terms, a matter of indifference to me, just as is his little soul or his little body. For even if we are born most especially for one another's sake, still each person's mind has its own sovereign power. Otherwise my neighbor's wickedness would make me wretched — which God has not willed, lest my misery should lie in another's power. The sun appears to spread itself everywhere, and indeed 57

BOOK VIII. 165

Just as if someone were to approach a clear and sweet spring and curse it, yet the spring would not cease to pour forth its drinkable water; and even if one threw mud or dung into it, the spring would quickly disperse these things, wash them away, and not be stained at all. How then will you have an ever-flowing spring rather than a mere well? [52] By training yourself at every hour toward freedom, with simplicity, and with dignity.

He who does not know that the world exists does not know where he is. He who does not know what he was born for does not know who he is, nor what the world is. He who has fallen short in any one of these things could not even say what he himself was born for. What would you think of one who flees the applause of those whose very name and whereabouts he does not know, nor even who they are?

[53] Do you want to be praised by a man who curses himself three times an hour? Do you want to please a man who does not please himself? Does the man who regrets nearly everything he does please himself?

[54] No longer merely breathe in sympathy with the air that surrounds you, but now also think in harmony with the universal intelligence that encompasses all things. For the intelligent power is no less diffused and permeates all things endowed with capacity, than the breath of air pervades all those capable of breathing.

[55] Vice in general does no harm to the universe. Vice in particular does no harm to another. It is harmful only to the one to whom it is granted to be free of it, whenever he first so wills.

[56] To my own rational faculty, the rational faculty of my neighbor is equally a matter of indifference, as is his breath or his little piece of flesh. For even if we were made especially for one another, still each of our ruling faculties has its own sovereignty; for otherwise my neighbor's vice would become my evil — which God did not see fit, lest my misfortune depend on another.

166 M. ANTONINI

The sun seems to pour itself out, and indeed it pours in every direction, yet it is not poured out. For this pouring is in fact a stretching. The rays are its beams, derived from the word for "extending." What a ray actually is, you could observe if sunlight enters through a narrow opening into a darkened room: it goes in a straight line, and as it were divides itself against whatever solid surface it meets, cutting off the air beyond; and there it stops, and neither slides away nor falls. Such must be the diffusion and spreading of the mind — not a pouring out at all, but a stretching; not making its pressure against obstacles violent or headlong, nor collapsing, but standing firm and illuminating what receives it. For that which does not transmit the light will deprive itself of it.

58. He who fears death fears either insensibility or a different kind of sensation. But if there is no longer sensation, there is also no sensation of any evil; or if you acquire a different kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of creature and will not cease to live.

59. Human beings exist for the sake of one another. So either teach them, or bear with them.

60. An arrow moves one way, the mind another. The mind, even when it pauses to take careful aim and considers its target, moves no less straight toward its objective.

61. To enter into the ruling faculty of each person; and to allow every other person likewise to enter into their own ruling faculty.

Whoever acts unjustly, acts impiously. For since universal nature has brought rational creatures into being for one another's sake, so that they may benefit one another according to each one's worth, and in no way harm one another, whoever violates this decree of nature acts altogether impiously against the most ancient of all divine laws. For the nature of the universe is the nature of all things. And all things that exist are bound together by a kind of mutual necessity. Moreover, this same principle, called nature, is also called truth, and is the first cause of all things that are true. Therefore, one who knowingly and willingly lies acts impiously, insofar as by deceiving he acts unjustly; and one who lies unwittingly and unknowingly acts impiously insofar as he dissents from universal nature and disrupts the beautifully ordered arrangement of the world, by acting against the nature of the world. For he acts against it who, as far as in him lies, is carried toward things that are contrary to truth. He had indeed once received from nature the means to discern truth, but having neglected these, he is now unable to distinguish the false from the true. Furthermore, one who pursues pleasures as though they were goods, and flees pain as though it were evil, also acts impiously. For it is inevitable that such a person will often complain about the nature of things, as though it assigns to good and bad alike more than they deserve; since the wicked often overflow with pleasures and abound in the things by which these are obtained, while the good on the contrary are worn down by pain and fall into circumstances of the kind that tend to produce suffering. Moreover, one who fears pain will fear some of the things that must necessarily come to pass in the world: and this is impious. And one who pursues pleasure will not refrain from doing injury: this

1. One who acts unjustly acts impiously. Furthermore, truth itself is the name given to this nature, and it is the first cause of all true things. For he had received from nature the means of discernment, which by neglecting he is no longer able to distinguish false things from true ones. Moreover, one who pursues pleasures as goods and flees pains as evils also acts impiously. For such a person must often find fault with the universal nature, as though it distributes things unequally to the base and to the worthy — since the base are often found in pleasures and acquire the means of obtaining them, while the worthy fall into pains and into the things that produce them. Furthermore, one who fears pains will sometimes fear something that is going to happen in the world; and this is already impious. And one who pursues pleasures will not refrain from acting unjustly; and this is openly impious.

And so everything that partakes of the common rational nature tends toward its kindred in the same way — or even more so. For the higher it is above other things, the more ready it is to blend and unite with what is akin to it. Among irrational creatures, then, we find herds, swarms, the rearing of young, and what might be called affections. Among rational animals there are city-states, friendships, households, assemblies, and in wars, treaties and truces. Among those yet higher — those that are, in a sense, already separated — a union was established, such as we see in the stars. Thus the ascent toward the higher was able to produce sympathy and work even among things widely separated. Consider what is now happening. Only rational beings have now forgotten their mutual striving and sense of unity, and here alone the flowing-together is not to be seen. Yet even when they flee from one another they are caught and held — for nature prevails. You will see what I mean if you watch carefully. For you will sooner find something earthy touching nothing earthy than you will find a human being cut off from all other humans. They are carried along. Every earthly thing is carried toward the earth by its own weight; all moisture flows together into one; likewise every airy thing does the same: so that some force is needed to keep them apart, to prevent this from happening. Fire is carried upward toward elemental fire; and everything here below is so ready to kindle along with it that all matter, being somewhat drier, is very apt to catch fire, because it has less moisture mixed into it — which would otherwise prevent combustion. Accordingly, whatever participates in intellectual nature is likewise drawn readily toward what is akin to it, or even much more so. For the more excellent a thing is compared to others, the more readily does it mingle with what is of its own kind and in some manner coalesce with it. And even among still more excellent beings — the stars, for instance, though separated from one another in a certain way — there nonetheless exists a kind of union. How many there are who do not even know your name; how many who will soon forget it; how many who now praise you but will soon find fault with you. In the end, neither memory, nor glory, nor anything of that sort is worthy of any consideration whatsoever.

31. Let tranquility of mind be yours in those things that arise from external causes. Let the principle of justice govern those things that arise from within. That is, let your intention and every action have this one goal set before it: to do whatever serves human society, as being consistent with your own nature.

32. You will be able to cut away many superfluous things that trouble you — for they exist entirely in your own judgment — and to open up great space for yourself, by grasping in your mind the whole world and all of time in which you live, by contemplating the rapid change of each individual thing, and how brief is the interval between the birth and the death of each thing; and how vast is the time that preceded its birth, and likewise how boundless is the time that will follow its end.

33. All that you see will soon perish; and those who witness this perishing will themselves soon perish. He who dies worn out by extreme old age is brought to the same condition as he who died before his time.

34. Look into the bare souls of men, and see what sort of minds they carry, what things they pursue, and for what reasons they love and honor some above others. Then consider how much arrogance accompanies their apparent efforts to harm someone through blame or to benefit someone through praise.

35. Loss is nothing other than change. And in change nature delights, for nature does nothing wrongly. All things have been thus from eternity; and to eternity such things will continue to come to be. Who then would say that all things have both always been made, and will always be made —

184 OF M. ANTONINUS

that evils would come to pass? nor that the Gods, however many they may be, had the power to correct these things, so that the world would not be given over to these evils, by which it would be perpetually entangled? How vile is the underlying matter of each thing: water, dust, little bones, filth; or again, the callosities of the earth, marble; sediment, gold and silver; hair, clothing; blood, purple; and whatever else of this kind. Even that which partakes of form is itself something of this same sort, and passes from one thing into another. Enough already of a calamitous life, of grumbling, and of trifles. Why are you troubled? What is new in these things? What at last strikes you down? Is it form? Look at it. Is it matter? Look at that too. Beyond these there is nothing. Be therefore at last somewhat more simple and better disposed toward the Gods. It matters not whether one has known these things for a hundred years or three. If anyone has gone wrong, the evil is in himself; though perhaps he has not even gone wrong. Or from one common mind, as from a common source, all things come upon a single body; and one ought not to complain of those parts which come from the whole; or atoms prevail, and there is nothing else but mixture and random dispersal. Why then are you troubled? Will you say to your mind: you are dead, you are corrupted, you dissemble, you have become like cattle, you graze like a beast, you have turned into a wild animal? Either the Gods can do nothing, or they can. If they can do nothing, why do you pray? If they can, why do you not rather ask of them through prayer that you desire none of these things, that you be anxious about none of them, rather than that any of these things happen or not happen? For if they can truly bring their help to mankind, they can help in these matters too. But you will say perhaps that the Gods have placed these things in your own power. Is it not then better to use with freedom those things that are in your power, than to pursue with servitude those things that are outside your power—

39. 40. Either the gods have no power, or they do have power. If they have no power, why pray? Well then, is it not better to use what is in your power with

186 M. ANTONINI

with freedom, or to struggle against things not in your power with servility and abasement? And who told you that the gods do not help us in matters that depend on us? Begin now to pray about these things. One man prays: "How may I sleep with that woman?" You pray: "How may I not desire to sleep with her?" Another: "How may I not lose my child?" You: "How may I not fear losing it?" Turn your desires in this direction, and see what comes of it. Epicurus says that during his illness he did not speak of the sufferings of his poor body with those who visited him, nor did he converse with them about such things. But he says he continued to discuss the principles of natural philosophy, and reflected on how the mind, even while sharing in such physical disturbances of the flesh, maintains its tranquility by preserving its own proper good. He says he did not allow the physicians to boast, as if they were accomplishing something great, but his life went on well and finely. Do the same as he did in illness, if you are ill, or in any other difficult circumstance. For not to abandon philosophy in whatever circumstances befall us, and not to talk nonsense with the ignorant or the mere natural philosopher, is common to every philosophical school, not only to the one now being practiced, nor to the instrument by which one acts. When you observe shamelessness in someone, ask yourself at once: is it possible that there be no shameless people in the world? It is not possible. Then do not require the impossible. For this person is one of those shameless ones who must necessarily exist in the world. The same applies to the rogue, the untrustworthy, and everyone who errs in whatever way — as soon as you remind yourself that it is impossible for such a kind not to exist, you will become more gentle toward the individual.

with anxiety and despondency of spirit? Although who would say that the Gods do not bring us aid even in those matters that lie within ourselves? Begin therefore to entreat the Gods with prayer, and you will see what will come of it. This man prays: how shall I manage to obtain that woman's favors? You pray: how shall I manage not to desire her favors? Another prays: how shall I rid myself of that man's authority? You pray: how shall I manage not to need to rid myself of it? Epicurus said: "When I lay ill, I did not spend my time in conversations about my bodily sufferings with those who visited me, nor did I speak to them of such matters. Rather, I continued to discuss the things I had previously studied concerning nature, and I applied myself especially to this: that my mind, even while sharing in the movements of my frail body, should nonetheless remain undisturbed and retain its own good." And he added that he did not allow the physicians to make much of themselves, as though they were doing something great, but that his life was going on as well as possible even then. Do you likewise, as he did, whether in illness if it should befall you, or in any other adverse circumstance. For it is common to every school of philosophy not to abandon philosophy in whatever circumstances arise, nor to idle along with the common people who are ignorant of the nature of things, but to attend only to the matter at hand and the means by which it is to be accomplished. When you are offended by someone's shamelessness, ask yourself at once: is it possible that there should be no shameless people in the world? It is not possible. Do not then ask for what cannot be. It is most useful also to consider within yourself what virtue nature has given to man against this fault. For she has given, as an antidote, gentleness against stupidity, and against each vice some corresponding faculty. And in general, you are entirely permitted to correct one who has been deceived and instruct him better. For whoever does wrong has gone astray from his purpose and has been deceived. What harm then has he done you? For you will find that none of those at whom you are angry has done anything to make your mind worse. Your evil and loss consist in this alone. And what evil or strange thing happens if an uneducated man acts as uneducated men do? Consider whether you ought not rather to blame yourself, for not having expected that he would commit this fault; for reason gave you sufficient grounds to think it probable that he would act so, yet you forgot this and are now surprised that he has done it. But above all, when you blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, turn the criticism upon yourself. For without doubt the fault is your own, whether you believed that a man of such a character would keep faith with you, or if you gave a benefit, you did not give it unconditionally, nor as one who had already received the full fruit of the action itself. For what more would you want after you have done good to a man? Is it not enough that you have acted in accordance with your nature? Do you seek a reward besides? It is as if the eye demanded payment for seeing, or the feet for walking. For just as these members are formed for a certain function, and having performed it according to their nature have obtained what is their own; so too man, being born to do good, when he has done something beneficial or contributed to the common good, has done that for which he was made, and has obtained what is his own.

Will you ever then, O my soul, be good, and simple, and one, and naked, more manifest than the body that surrounds you? Will you ever taste of a loving and contented disposition? Will you ever be full and without want, craving nothing, desiring nothing — neither animate nor inanimate things for the enjoyment of pleasures — nor time in which to enjoy them longer, nor place or region or favorable climate, nor harmony of men? But will you be satisfied with your present condition, and pleased with all that is present, and persuade yourself that all things are present to you, all things are well with you, and that they come from the gods, and that all shall be well — whatever is pleasing to them, and whatever they shall give for the preservation of that perfect living being, which is good and just and beautiful, which generates all things and holds all things together, and encompasses all things, and takes into itself all things that are dissolved for the generation of others like them? Will you ever then be such as to be able to live as a citizen together with gods and men, neither finding fault with them, nor being condemned by them? Observe what your nature as a mere natural being requires, and do it and accept it, if your nature as a living creature is not made worse thereby. Next you must observe what your nature as a living creature requires, and accept all of that, if your nature as a rational living creature is not made worse thereby. Now the rational is also straightway the social. Use these rules then, and trouble yourself about nothing further. Everything that happens either happens in such a way that you are naturally formed to bear it, or in such a way that you are not naturally formed

BOOK X.

1 When will you be good, O soul, simple, one, naked, clearer than the body that surrounds you? When will you taste the disposition given over to genuine love and affection? When will you be full, wanting for nothing, desiring nothing further, neither animate nor inanimate thing by which to take pleasure, no further time in which to enjoy it longer, no other place, or region, or gentle climate of the sky, or friendly company of people? But rather will you be content with your present condition, and delight in all things present, and be persuaded that all things are at hand for you, that all things are well for you; and that they come from the Gods, and that you will fare well in whatever they have seen fit to grant, and whatever they are going to grant, as things that conduce to the welfare of a being perfect, upright, just, and honest — one which generates, contains, embraces, and encompasses all those things which, like other similar things, arise from that same source and dissolve back into it? When will you be so disposed as to live among gods and men in such a way that you neither bring any charge against them nor are condemned by them yourself?

2 Observe what your nature requires, insofar as it is governed by nature alone. Do this and allow it, unless your nature as an animal would thereby become worse. Then observe what your nature as an animal requires. Grant yourself this too, unless your nature as a rational being would thereby become worse.

3 But what is rational is also straightway social. Using these rules, strive for nothing further. Whatever happens, either it happens in such a way that you are by nature fitted to bear it, or in such a way that you are not. If it happens that you are fitted to bear it, then —

192 M. Antoninus

Do not bear it with reluctance, but carry it as you were born to carry it. But if it should happen that you were not born to bear it, do not let even that weigh upon you; for where it will have consumed you, it will destroy itself as well. Remember, however, that by nature you are fitted to bear whatever it is that your own judgment places before you, making it tolerable, or judging it to be either advantageous to you or a matter of duty to perform it. 4 If anyone is in error, gently show him his mistake by teaching him. But if you cannot do this, blame yourself — or not even yourself. 5 Whatever befalls you was destined for you from eternity: and the intertwined series of causes has from eternity woven together your very existence with that particular event. 6 Whether atoms govern all things, or nature rules the universe, let this first be established: that I am a part of the whole, which is governed by nature. Next, that I am bound by a certain kinship to the other parts of the same kind. Keeping this in mind — insofar as I am a part of the whole — I shall not be vexed at anything assigned to me by the universe. For nothing can be harmful to the part that is beneficial to the whole; and the universe contains nothing that is not conducive to itself. Since all natures share this in common, and the nature of the world goes still further in that it cannot be compelled by any external cause to produce anything harmful to itself — when I remember, therefore, that I am a part of such a universe, whatever happens will be welcome and acceptable to me. And insofar as I am bound by a certain kinship to parts of the same kind, I will do nothing that violates the law of fellowship; rather, I will have regard for those akin to me, and direct all my efforts toward what is beneficial to the common good, and abstain from what is contrary to it. With these things thus accomplished, my life must necessarily flow prosperously — just as one would judge a citizen's life to flow prosperously if he has steadfastly carried out those actions that are beneficial to his fellow citizens of the same city, and whatever the city

to bear it by nature. If it so happens that you bear it as nature intended, do not be troubled; but bear it as nature intended. If, however, you bear it contrary to nature, do not be troubled; for it will consume and destroy you. Remember, however, that you are capable of bearing everything, because it is within your own judgment to make it bearable and endurable, by imagining that it is beneficial or fitting for you to do so. If someone errs, correct them gently, and point out what is being overlooked. But if you are unable, blame yourself — or not even yourself. Whatever happens to you was prepared for you from eternity; and the interweaving of causes has spun together both your very existence from all time, and this event's occurrence. Whether there be atoms or natures, let this be first established: that I am a part of the whole governed by nature. Next, that I stand in a certain close relationship to the parts that are of the same kind. Remembering these things, insofar as I am a part, I shall be discontented with nothing that is apportioned from the whole. For nothing is harmful to the part that is beneficial to the whole. For the whole contains nothing that is not beneficial to itself — this being common to all natures; and the nature of the universe has this additional property, that it cannot be compelled by any external cause to generate anything harmful to itself. Inasmuch, then, as I remember that I am a part of such a whole, I shall be content with everything that comes to pass. And insofar as I stand in a close relationship to the kindred parts, I shall do nothing unsocial; rather I shall direct my attention to those of the same kind, and direct every impulse toward the common good, and away from its opposite. With these principles thus carried out, life must flow smoothly — just as you would find the life of a citizen flowing, one who advances through actions that benefit his fellow citizens, and whatever the city

194 M. ANTONINI

...a city assigns, we must be content with. For the parts of the whole — all those, I say, that are encompassed by the universe — must necessarily perish; and let this be understood as signifying their transformation. If, however, it is (I say) an evil and a harmful thing for them, then the whole could not proceed well, since its parts would be moving toward alienation and variously disposed toward destruction. Did nature itself undertake to make its own parts evil, and to make them susceptible to evil, and by necessity to lead them into evil — or did it fail to notice that such was the case? Both alternatives are implausible. But if someone, setting aside nature altogether, were to explain these things as simply following their inherent constitution, how absurd it would be to marvel or be vexed at what happens as though it were contrary to nature — and this, moreover, when dissolution into those same elements from which each thing was composed is taking place. For it is either a scattering of the elements from which the thing was combined, or a transformation — the solid part passing into earth, and the breath-like part into air — so that these too are taken up again into the rational principle of the whole, whether by a periodic conflagration or by eternal alternating renewal. Do not, then, imagine that the solid and the breath-like parts have existed since one's birth. For all of this received its influx only yesterday or the day before, from food and the air drawn in. What it has thus received, it transforms — and so too with what one's mother bore. Suppose, however, that that concern clings too closely to what is properly one's own — I consider it nothing relevant to what is now being said. Give yourself these names: good, modest, truthful, prudent, cooperative, high-minded — and take care that you never change those names, and quickly lose those titles —

7Whatever the state has attributed to him, let him receive it with gratitude. All the parts of the universe, as many as are contained within its compass, must necessarily undergo corruption. By corruption I mean alteration. Now since this is necessary, if it were also harmful to them, it would surely be more fitting to proceed with the whole, since its parts were frequently undergoing alteration and were constituted in many ways for dissolution. Shall we say, then, that nature itself has arranged its parts to be afflicted by evil, and so formed them that they were not only naturally liable to fall into evil, but would fall into it of necessity? Or that they were made so by nature itself in secret? Neither is plausible. But if one, setting aside the name of nature, should wish to say they are born thus, see how absurd it is that the one who says the parts of the universe are born to change should wonder and be troubled at this very thing — their changing — as if it were something contrary to the nature of things themselves; especially (to pass over other considerations) since each thing is resolved back into those elements from which it was composed. For there is either a dispersal of the elements from which it had been compounded, or a conversion — whatever is solid goes to earth, whatever is airy goes to air — so that these too are taken back into the rational principle of the whole, whether it is consumed by fire after a fixed revolution of time, or perpetually renewed by unceasing cycles of change. Do not imagine, furthermore, that the solid or airy part is what existed from the very beginning. For all that you now have flowed in only yesterday and the day before, from food and the air you breathed in. So what changes is what was received after birth, not what your mother originally brought forth. Even granting that this particular attachment to what is so disposed is very strong in you, nothing will stand in the way of what has already been said being true. When you have taken to yourself the names of good, temperate, truthful, prudent, harmonious, magnanimous, take care never to exchange them—

196 M. Antoninus

bear these names, and if you lose them again, return to them quickly (should such a thing occur). Remember that the name "prudent" signifies for you careful consideration of each individual matter and diligent attention. The name "of one mind" signifies the spontaneous embrace of all things assigned by universal nature. The name "magnanimous" signifies the elevation of the mind above every gentle or harsh affection of the flesh, above petty glory, above death, and above all such things. If therefore you keep yourself within these names, and do not desire that others honor you with these titles, you will soon be a different person than you once were, and will enter upon a different way of life. For to persist as you have been, and to wallow and be torn apart shamefully in such a life, belongs to a man utterly devoid of feeling and too greedily clinging to life — not unlike those beast-fighters who, half-eaten and covered with wounds and filth, beg to be kept alive until the next day, only to be thrown to the same claws and bites once again. Commit yourself therefore to these few names. And if indeed you can persist in them, persist, as though translated to certain islands of the blessed. But if you feel you are falling away and cannot maintain your footing, withdraw boldly to some corner where you may still do something. Or even depart from life altogether — not in anger, but simply, freely, modestly — having accomplished this one thing alone worthy of remembrance in life: that you departed from it in such a manner. To help you remember these names, it will be of great benefit to remember the gods, and that they do not wish those endowed with reason to flatter them, but to become like them; and to remember that a fig tree does what a fig tree does, a dog does what a dog does, a bee does what a bee does — and likewise a human being does what a human being does. those doctrines which the natural philosopher imagines and passes along. One must look at and do everything in such a way that either the practical element is accomplished at the same time, or the contemplative element is exercised simultaneously, or the self-confident sense arising from knowledge of each thing is felt openly, not hidden. For at one time you enjoy simplicity, at another dignity, at another the knowledge proper to each thing — what it is in its essence, what place it holds in the universe, how long it is naturally destined to endure, of what elements it is composed, who can possess it, and who can give or take it away.

One man prides himself on having caught a spider, another a little hare, another a small fish in a net, another bears, another Sarmatians. Are these not the ones you will choose, if you examine their principles? How all things change into one another — acquire a contemplative method, or attend to this continually, or exercise yourself in this area. For nothing is more productive of true greatness of mind. He put off the body, and reflecting that soon, when departing from among men, he would have to leave all these things behind, he gave himself wholly — in matters depending on himself to justice, and in all other things that befall him to the nature of the whole. As for what anyone might say or think about him, or do against him, he did not even take it into his mind. Content with these two things only — to act justly in what is presently appointed, and to love what is presently allotted to him — he let go of all other occupations and distractions, and wished for nothing other than to walk the straight path according to the law, and to follow God who walks the straight path.

When a spider catches a fly, it boasts as if it had accomplished something great; another man, when he has caught a hare, another when he has netted a fish, another when he has caught boars, another bears, another Sarmatians. For what do these hunters differ from brigands, if you examine the principles and intentions on both sides? 11. Let yourself be trained in the contemplative method, by which you may have a clear view of how all things change into one another. Apply yourself to this constantly, and exercise yourself in this above all else. For nothing contributes more to the elevation of the mind. One who is so disposed strips away the body, and reflecting that he must soon depart from all these things and from the company of men, gives himself over entirely to justice in what he himself does, and to universal nature in what befalls him. As for what anyone else may say or think of him, or do against him, he does not so much as think of it — being content with just these two things: to act justly in all his present actions, and to embrace whatever is presently allotted to him; setting aside all other business and pursuits, desiring nothing other than to go forward rightly according to the law, and 12. to follow God himself as he goes forward. What use is there for suspicion, when what ought to be done lies ready to hand? And if you have indeed seen clearly what that is, proceed with it calmly and steadily; if not, stop and seek the best...

208 M. ANTONINUS

Whatever is given to you to do according to your nature is given everywhere. For indeed a cylinder is not permitted to move of its own accord in every direction; nor is water, nor fire, nor anything else governed by mere nature or an irrational soul. For there are many things that restrain and obstruct them. But the mind and reason proceed through every obstacle just as it was born to do, and just as it wills. Therefore, keeping this before your eyes, seek nothing further — reason moves through all things with the same ease as fire moves upward, a stone downward, a cylinder along a slope. The remaining obstacles are either of the body, which it holds after the manner of a corpse, or, being removed by opinion and the inclination of reason, they do not break it or cause any harm. For otherwise, the one who suffers them would become worse. Indeed, in all other endeavors it is so that whatever evil befalls any of them makes worse the thing affected by it. But here, if one may say so, a person becomes more excellent and more worthy of praise when he makes right use of what is thrown in his way. In summary, remember: a native citizen harms nothing unless he harms the city; the city harms nothing unless it harms the law. Now, of those things we call misfortunes, none harms the law. But what does not harm the law harms neither the city nor the citizen. One who is imbued with true principles will find it sufficient to be reminded by this brief saying, snatched from the commonplace, for driving away grief or fear — such as this:

The rough force of the wind strews some leaves upon the ground:
But nature prepares others, which grow green in spring.
Such is the race of men: this one is born, that one dies.

They will soon be gone. To a cylinder, the impulse to roll in any direction gives its own characteristic motion; so too with water, with fire, and with all other things governed by nature or by irrational soul — for the obstacles and resistances they encounter are many. But mind and reason are able throughout to make their way through everything that opposes them, just as their nature and will require. Keep before your eyes this ease with which reason moves through all things — as fire moves upward, as a stone falls downward, as a cylinder rolls along a slope — and seek nothing further. For the remaining obstacles belong either to the dead body, or arise without any judgment involved, or come from reason's own yielding — and that which crushes or harms in such a way does no harm at all; for indeed, if the one who suffers were made worse by it, he would immediately have become a bad person. In the case of all other constructed things, whatever ill befalls any of them, the thing that suffers becomes worse for it; but here, if one must say so, the human being actually becomes better and more praiseworthy, by rightly using whatever befalls him. And in general, remember this: nothing harms one who is by nature a citizen, that does not harm the city; nor does anything harm the city that does not harm the law. Of those things called misfortunes, none harms the law. What does not harm the law, therefore, harms neither city nor citizen. For one who has been trained by true doctrines, even the briefest saying, ready at hand, suffices as a reminder against grief and fear. For example:

Leaves — some the wind scatters on the ground, while others
the flourishing forest brings forth when spring's season comes on:
so it is with the generation of men — one springs up, another passes away.

BOOK XI.

The properties of the rational soul: it sees itself, it articulates itself, it makes itself whatever it wishes, it reaps the fruit it bears. (For the fruits of plants, and the analogous case in animals, are reaped by others.) It achieves its own proper end wherever the limit of life may overtake it. Unlike dancing or acting or similar activities, where the whole performance is incomplete if something interrupts it — but at every part, and wherever it may be overtaken, it renders what has been assigned to it full and wanting nothing, so that it can say: I have what is mine. Moreover, it ranges through the whole universe, and the void surrounding it, and its form, and it extends into the infinity of time, and encompasses, comprehends, and contemplates the periodic regeneration of all things — seeing that those who come after us will see nothing newer, and those before us saw nothing more remarkable; but in a way a man of forty, if he has any understanding at all, has seen everything past and future according to its essential sameness. It is also proper to the rational soul to love one's neighbor, and truth, and modesty, and to value nothing above itself — which is proper to law as well; and thus right reason and the reason of justice are no different from one another.

2. You will come to despise a pleasing song, or dancing, or the all-round athletic contest, if you break up the melodious voice into each of its individual notes and ask yourself whether you are overcome by each one separately — for you will be abashed. And doing the same with dancing, movement by movement,
