1 These are the properties of the soul endowed with reason. It sees itself, it shapes and constrains itself as it wishes, and whatever it wills, it makes itself to be: it gathers for itself the fruit it produces. Whereas the fruits of trees, and whatever corresponds to them in animals, are gathered by others — the rational soul always attains its own end, wherever the boundary of life is set. For it is not the case here as in dancing or acting in a play or similar pursuits, where, if something goes wrong, the whole performance is left incomplete; but in whatever part and wherever it may be found, what has gone before it makes fully complete and perfect in itself — so that one may truly say: "What is mine, I have entirely." Moreover, it ranges over the whole world, and contemplates the void that surrounds it, and reaches out into the immensity of time, and grasps and considers the renewal of the universe at fixed intervals; and it perceives at once that our descendants will see nothing new, just as our ancestors saw nothing more than we have — so that in a sense, one who has lived forty years, possessed of any degree of intelligence and having observed the course of events, has, by the law of uniformity, seen all things past and future alike. These too are properties of the rational soul: to love one's neighbors, to be truthful and modest, to prefer nothing above itself — which is also the property of law — so that between right reason and the reason of justice there is no difference. You will scorn a pleasant song, dancing, and wrestling, if, dividing each by its individual notes or movements with a harmonious voice, you ask yourself of each in turn: "Does this master me?" — for you would blush to admit it. So likewise with the individual movements and gestures of the dance, and with wrestling too, if you do the same,

If you have done this, it will come about that you are likewise disposed toward these afflictions; and so, having accepted virtue alone and the actions of virtue, remember in all other things to return to the individual points considered separately, so that through their disjunction you may hold those very things in contempt — and transfer this same practice to your life as a whole. What kind of soul is it that is ready, here and now, if need be, to depart from the body, and to be either extinguished, or scattered, or to remain? 3 I mean ready in such a way that this readiness flows from one's own reasoned judgment, not from mere stubbornness, after the manner of the Christians — so that you may face death calmly, composedly, without tumult, and in a way that you could also persuade others to do the same. Have I done something for the common good? 4 I have thereby received a benefit. Let this thought always come to your aid, and never cease from it. What is the art you profess? 5 The art of living well. How is this better accomplished than through the aid of teachings, some of which concern the universal nature, and others the particular condition of man? Tragedies were originally introduced 6 to remind men of the chances and events of life, so that they might be warned that such things naturally come to pass; and so that they would not bear heavily in the greater theater of life those things by which they were delighted on the stage — since they would have seen that these things cannot be otherwise, and that even those who cry out "Alas, O Cithaeron!" must endure them. And indeed certain useful things are said by dramatic poets, such as above all this:

If the Gods neglect me and my children, there is a reason even for this.

All those things which you pray to attain through a long circuit, you can have right now, if you do not begrudge them to yourself. That is, if you leave behind all that is past, entrust the future to Providence, and direct only the present toward holiness and justice. Holiness, so that you may love what is allotted to you — for nature brought it, and it was meant for this — and justice, so that you may speak the truth freely and without evasion, and do what is in accordance with law and with worth. Let nothing hinder you: neither another's vice, nor opinion, nor the voice, nor even the sensation of the flesh that has grown around you — for it will see the thickness. Whenever you are at the point of departure, having left all else behind, if you honor only your ruling faculty and the divine within you, and fear not the ceasing to live but rather the never having begun to live according to nature — then you will stand as a person worthy of the universe that gave you birth, and you will cease to be a stranger in your own homeland, marveling as if unexpected at the things that happen every day, hanging upon this and that.

What remains last is simply to obey God and reason. Yet this principle is contradicted if anyone takes it hard that he must be parted from these things by death. How small a portion of infinite and boundless time is assigned to each person? For it is swallowed up with the greatest swiftness from an endless expanse. How small a part, too, of all matter? Nothing will more strongly inspire contempt for death than to reflect that even those who count pleasure among good things and pain among evils have nevertheless despised death. For one who regards only what is timely as good, and who thinks it makes no difference whether he has performed more or fewer actions in accordance with right reason, or has contemplated the universe for a longer or shorter span of time — for such a person death cannot be terrible. But in life, three acts can make a complete play. For he who determines its end is the same one who was once the author of its composition and is now the author of its dissolution. Letter of Antoninus to the Assembly of Asia concerning our religion.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, Armenicus, Pontifex Maximus, holding the Tribunician Power for the fifteenth time, Consul for the third time, to the Assembly of Asia, Greetings. The Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, Germanicus, Parthicus, Sarmaticus, to the Roman people and the sacred Senate, greetings. I have informed you of the magnitude of my undertaking, and of what kinds of hardships and troubles afflicted me at the borders of Germany amid the surrounding enemy camps, with myself encircled by seventy cohorts within a space of nine miles at Cotinum. 1 A letter of Marcus to his prefect, informing him that he has entrusted the Syrian legions to Avidius Cassius.

I have given the Syrian legions to Avidius Cassius — legions dissolute with luxury and conducting themselves after the manner of Daphne, all of whom Coesonius Vectilianus reports he found utterly debauched. And I think I have not erred, since you yourself know Cassius well — a man of Cassian strictness and discipline. For soldiers cannot be governed except by old-fashioned discipline. You know the verse spoken by a good poet and repeated by everyone: "By ancient customs and her men Rome stands." You need only ensure that the legions are abundantly supplied with provisions, which, if I know Avidius well, I am confident will not be wasted.

The Reply of the Prefect to Marcus.

You have decided rightly, my lord, in placing Cassius in command of the Syrian legions. For nothing is so useful as a rather strict man for soldiers of Greek habits. He will certainly shake off all their self-indulgences, all the flowers from head, neck, and breast of the soldier. All military provisions are ready, and nothing is lacking under a good commander: for not much is either sought or spent.

A Letter of Verus to M. Antoninus.

Avidius Cassius is ambitious for power, as it seems to me, and he made himself known already in the time of my grandfather, your father — I would urge you to have him watched. He finds everything of ours displeasing, he is amassing considerable wealth, he mocks our literary pursuits. He calls you an old woman philosopher, and me a dissolute fool. Consider what must be done: I do not hate the man, but take care lest upon you and your children

LETTERS. 257

does not serve your interests well, since you have among your guard such men as soldiers willingly hear and willingly look upon.

The Reply of Marcus Concerning Avidius Cassius.

I have read your letter, and found it anxious rather than imperial, and not of our times. For if empire is owed to him by divine will, we shall not be able to kill him, even if we wish to. You know the saying of your great-grandfather: no one kills his own successor. If that is not the case, then he will of his own accord, without any cruelty on our part, fall into the fatal snare. Add to this that we cannot make a criminal of one whom no one accuses and whom (as you yourself say) the soldiers love. Moreover, in cases of treason it is the nature of things that even those against whom it is proved seem to suffer violence. You know yourself what your grandfather Hadrian said: Wretched is the condition of emperors, for the charge of seeking tyranny cannot be believed against them unless they are killed. I preferred to cite his example rather than that of Domitian, who is said to have first uttered this. For even the good sayings of tyrants do not carry as much authority as they deserve. Let him then keep his own ways, especially since he is a good general, strict and brave, and necessary to the state. As for your saying that my children must be protected by his death — let my children perish outright if Avidius shall deserve to be loved more than they, and if it shall serve the state better that Cassius live than the sons of Marcus.

The Letter of Marcus to the Empress Faustina.

Verus had written me the truth about Avidius — that he desired to reign. I believe you have heard what the informers reported about him. Come therefore to Albanum, so that we may discuss everything, the gods willing, fearing nothing.

I myself will come to Albanum tomorrow, as you command: but I urge you now, if you love your children, to pursue these rebellions most vigorously. For both commanders and soldiers have grown accustomed to bad ways — those who are not suppressed will themselves become oppressors.

Another Letter of the Same Faustina to Marcus.

My mother Faustina urged your father Pius in the same way during the revolt of Celsus, that he should first keep faith with his own family, and so also with strangers. For an emperor is not truly devoted to duty who does not think of his wife and children. You see at what age our Commodus is: Pompejanus is both older than him and a foreigner. Consider carefully what you must do about Avidius Cassius and his accomplices. Do not spare men who have not spared you, and who would not have spared me or our children had they been victorious. I will soon follow you on your journey: because our Fadilla was ill, I could not come to Formianum. But if I cannot find you at Formiae, I will follow you to Capua, which city may help both my illness and that of our children. I ask that you send the physician Soteridam to Formianum. As for Pisitheus, I have no faith in him at all — he does not know how to apply proper treatment to a young girl. Calphurnius has given me sealed letters, to which if I am delayed in replying, I will do so through the old eunuch Caecilius, a man (as you know) of proven loyalty: to him I will give verbal instructions about what the wife of Avidius Cassius, his sons, and his son-in-law are reportedly boasting concerning you.

Antoninus

Antoninus's Reply.

You indeed, my Faustina, act dutifully on behalf of your husband and our children. For I have re-read your letter from Formiae, in which you urge me to take vengeance on those who were accomplices of Avidius. But I will spare both his children and his son-in-law and his wife, and I will write to the Senate so that the proscription may not be too harsh, nor the punishment too cruel. For there is nothing that better recommends a Roman emperor to the nations than clemency. This made Caesar a god, this consecrated Augustus, this above all adorned your father with the name of Pius. Indeed, if the matter of the war had been decided according to my judgment, not even Avidius would have been killed. Be at ease therefore; the gods watch over me, and my devotion to the gods is dear to their hearts. I have named our Pompeianus consul for the following year.

From the Speech of Marcus Antoninus Sent to the Senate.

You have therefore, Conscript Fathers, in place of congratulations for the victory, my son-in-law as consul. I mean Pompeianus, whose age long deserved to be rewarded with the consulship, had not brave men intervened, to whom what was owed to the state had to be rendered. Now as regards the defection of Cassius, I beg and beseech you, Conscript Fathers, to set aside your severity and uphold my sense of duty and mercy — indeed your own: let the Senate put no one to death. Let no senator be punished, let no nobleman's blood be shed; let the exiled return, let the proscribed recover their property. Would that I could recall many even from the dead. For vengeance for one's personal grievance is never becoming in an emperor: even if it were quite just, it appears excessive. Therefore you will grant pardon to the sons of Avidius Cassius, and to his son-in-law and his wife. And why do I say pardon? Since they have done nothing wrong. Let them therefore live in safety, knowing that under

P. 3. * The earlier reading was "I would apply my mind to matters of that sort," which does not adequately render the force of the Greek word ἐπιοθόαι. For this word is used of one who is scarcely in his right mind due to an insane passion for something, and it is especially used to denote the madness of lovers. So Lucian uses it: "madly in love with women," and in the fragment of Sappho quoted by Longinus: "It has made my heart flutter in my breast," which Catullus translates: "which wretched for me tears away all my senses."

P. 4. † Gatak. translates it as "I would have abstained from studies." Nor do the Stoics require this of their disciples, since as Seneca says (Epistle 88), liberal studies are useful only insofar as they prepare the mind, not when they detain it.

PAGE 33. Note 1. This is a Stoic doctrine: that it is permissible, indeed obligatory, to withdraw oneself from life on occasion. They called this a "reasonable departure," when what they considered just cause for emigrating from life was given. See Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, Book 1, and Laertius on Zeno. They say that the wise man may irrationally withdraw himself from life for the sake of his country, or for friends, or even if he finds himself in the most grievous pain, or mutilation, or incurable disease. P. 101. ¹ Galenus, on the authority of Stephanus, defines Hexis as "a spirit holding together and uniting the parts" — that spirit which binds and contains the parts: and by the term spiritus the word forma (form) is denoted. Hexis therefore in this place signifies either the bodily structure, the bare life-form, or rather the pure form itself, that is, the spirit of the vital faculty — what Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians, Book 8, ch. 2, calls a bare hexis, i.e., bare existence, and which Marcus here distinguishes from nature (φύσις). Philo also, in his work on the immortality of the world, establishes four grades of natural things: hexis, physis, psyche, nous — the hexis of stones, the physis of plants, the psyche of animals, the nous of humans — in exactly the same order as Marcus here; and, lest anything be lacking from what Marcus mentions, he adds: "and virtue, the most perfect of rational beings." Gataker. Antoninus divides substances endowed with soul into three classes. The first encompasses brute animals. The second includes many of the human race, who indeed possess rational souls, yet appear to go no further than being skilled in the arts and apt at producing refined works. The third finally comprises truly wise men, with illustrious, pure, and light-filled souls, akin to and resembling God, of whose genuine particles they feel themselves to be a part. In the Nekyia — that is, among those things believed to occur in the underworld (whence in the Odyssey, book 11, the name Νεκύας is attached) — things are enacted by representation, performed more effectively, and affect the minds of spectators more powerfully (thus Plato in the Laws: "rushing toward the souls"). Suidas mentions a festival or solemn occasion celebrated by the Greeks called the Nekyia; in which spectacles of this sort were perhaps exhibited. The Nekyia, he says, is the festival of the dead. Antoninus accordingly pronounces human affairs and the occupations of mortals to be in part similar — indeed entirely equal — to the games and quarrels of children, and in part to vain spectacles that tend to affect the minds of simpler people. Gataker. That Ulysses descended to the Underworld, and what intercourse he had with the dead, is depicted at length in the eleventh book of the Odyssey (to which book the name Νεκύας accordingly adheres), and I believe this is known to every reader. Hence it appears that Antoninus too borrowed his own image from this source. Whatever is done in human affairs is all merely a Stage and a Spectacle; not the things themselves, but representations of things. So far do we agree with those in the Underworld, that on both sides there are displayed only Shades and empty Phantoms of things. With this one difference, however: that what we encounter here are thick and tangible, whereas those below are thin and altogether elude the touch. And Sophocles had already said this long before, in his Ajax:

"For I see that all of us who live are nothing more
than phantoms, or an insubstantial shadow." Dacier.

Moreover, that body must expand, and both that new matter and the original matter must undergo yet another change — I mean Death, which will soon dissolve both back into their respective elements." Such is Dacerius; but how this interpretation can be drawn from the actual words I do not see, nor does the meaning (with all respect to that distinguished man) appear to suit the passage. Let us therefore consider whether something more fitting can be worked out. We can do no better than to begin by investigating the true and genuine meaning of those words τῷ ἰδίως ποιῷ, which the Interpreters seem not to have understood sufficiently. Τὸ ἰδίως ποιόν is that quality, or rather that bundle of qualities (as the philosophers call it), which is proper and peculiar to each individual and by which one is distinguished from all others. Now ποιαπλέκη τῷ ἰδίως ποιῷ denotes that from which this distinctive mark and character proper to each individual arises — something that binds each person strongly to this particular quality and holds him, as it were, wrapped up in it. The words therefore may be rendered in this sense: "Granted, however, that this (he means matter) is what binds you so forcefully to that particular quality and mark by which you are distinguished from all others, I nevertheless hold that this is no obstacle to what has already been said" — namely, that matter changes from hour to hour, and that new matter daily joins the body of any individual while other matter departs. For the objection commonly raised against the view of the perpetual flux of matter in bodies arises here: that each individual's distinctive mark and character derives from matter, and therefore it is not plausible that the character should change when the matter does not. He does not refute this objection — perhaps he could not, hurrying as he was — but simply says it carries no weight in his judgment. No small additional support for this interpretation may perhaps be found in a passage of Origen cited in Epiphanius (p. 536, Vol. 1, Edit. Par. 1622), where this very opinion

Defending this position, Origen uses these words: "And beyond these things, if there is something similar in this form, by which Peter or Paul is shaped — that corporeal quality which in the resurrection is again clothed upon the soul — changing further toward the better, which surely still retains something according to the first underlying subject." Moreover, although that bodily form is similar, by which Peter and Paul are chiefly constituted, and what is again given in the resurrection of the soul is converted to something better, nevertheless the matter itself which was first inherent in the body is not the same. Here it is worth noting that Origen is responding to nearly the same objection here as Marcus responds to there; and further, that what Antoninus calls the "individual quality," Origen calls the "form," by which Peter is shaped, etc. The corporeal quality, that bodily form or species by which Peter is constituted and distinguished from all others: which he also calls a little above "the form that characterizes the body," and likewise "the bodily quality of Peter or Paul," according to which quality the materials from childhood are shaped in the bodies, along with certain other individual characteristics. Finally, on the next page he uses a word coined from Marcus's own words, where he calls that which is peculiar to each person's form and character "that which individualizes the flesh." Marcus also below, at 12.30, uses "in their own particular bodies" to refer to bodies distinguished from one another by their peculiar qualities or properties. 9 I write: "even if you lose these bodies, quickly," etc. Casaubon.

PAGE 250. Note 1. This letter is taken from Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 13. It also exists in Justin Martyr, at the end of the Apology, though not in exactly the same words. Valesius, in his note on the passage, affirms that this letter, attributed by Eusebius to Antoninus Pius, belongs to our Marcus. 2 In this way Cicero spoke of the "Common Council of the Milyans" and the "Common Council of all Sicily" in the Verrine orations. Moreover, when the "koinon of Asia" is mentioned, the word "synedrion" is to be understood. For the Asians had a common Council of the entire people, to which individual cities sent delegates or synedri, as Aristides teaches in the 4th Sacred Oration. This reading pleases me greatly. However, Valesius's and Langus's translation is by no means approved by the most learned Grabe, who translates the final clause as: "and impute your own misfortunes to them."

CONTENTS
Of the First Volume of
An Essay on the Composition and Writings of the Ancients, Particularly PLATO.
[To be published soon.]

Section I. On the composition or structure of style; the positioning of words and the arrangement of sentences. Rules of this composition — from whom they are to be learned — and how a correct sense of taste is lost.

Section II. The different kinds of composition. — How poetry is to be introduced into prose. — The Ancients imitated Homer.

Section III. Xenophon's style. — How he imitates Homer.

Section IV. The style of Herodotus. — He also imitates Homer.

Section V. Thucydides' style. — He imitates the Pindaric manner.

Section VI. Plato's manner of writing is best understood by considering what he regards as the true purpose of eloquence, and the rules for achieving it. — Aristotle gives the same rules. — Plato's moral character.

Y y                    Sect.

CONTENTS.

SECTION VII. Plato adapts his reasoning to the character of his audience. — To what extent he practices skepticism. — His style in refutative dialogue. — The character of some of his dialogues.

SECTION VIII. The interconnection of Plato's dialogues considered — they are the best source of commentary on one another. — His reasons for joining natural philosophy to ethics. — Plato separated anger from divine justice.

SECTION IX. Mr. Warburton's division of Plato's dialogues into exoteric and esoteric examined and shown to be without foundation: as is also the conclusion he draws from it, that Plato did not believe in a future state of rewards and punishments.

SECTION X. Plato's style is frequently poetic. He imitates Homer in the beauties of descriptive poetry. — A defense offered for criticisms of this kind.

SECTION XI. Plato imitates Homer in his allegories. — An allegory concerning theology, morals, and politics.

SECTION XII. The Philosopher's Cave explained. — Plato did not hold that the soul is absorbed into the Deity after death. Mr. Warburton's assertion of this is shown to be without foundation.

SECTION XIII. A comparison of Homer's and Plato's similes.

SECTION XIV. Plato's descriptions of the passions, and how he imitates Homer in some of them.

SECTION.

CONTENTS.

SECTION XV. Philosophy, insofar as it acquaints us with the motivating forces behind human actions, is useful to an Orator. — Demosthenes studied Plato carefully. — His style. — A short defense of Isocrates.

SECTION XVI. Demosthenes often imitates Plato's manner in his descriptions, sentiments, and figures. The public virtues are strongly recommended by both. — Longinus also imitates Plato.
